tools.name: exec

format.definition:
start: pragma_source | plain_source
pragma_source: PRAGMA_LINE NEWLINE SOURCE
plain_source: SOURCE

PRAGMA_LINE: /[ \t]*\/\/ @exec:[^\r\n]*/
NEWLINE: /\r?\n/
SOURCE: /[\s\S]+/

tools.name: wait
tools.description:
Waits on a yielded `exec` cell and returns new output or completion.
- Use `wait` only after `exec` returns `Script running with cell ID ...`.
- `cell_id` identifies the running `exec` cell to resume.
- `yield_time_ms` controls how long to wait for more output before yielding again. Defaults to 10000 ms.
- `max_tokens` limits how much new output this wait call returns. Defaults to 10000 tokens.
- `terminate: true` stops the running cell; false or omitted waits for output.
- `wait` returns only the new output since the last yield, or the final completion or termination result for that cell.
- If the cell is still running, `wait` may yield again with the same `cell_id`.
- If the cell has already finished, `wait` returns the completed result and closes the cell.

cell_id.description: Identifier of the running exec cell.

max_tokens.description: Output token budget for this wait call. Defaults to 10000 tokens.

terminate.description: True stops the running exec cell; false or omitted waits for output.

yield_time_ms.description: Wait before yielding more output. Defaults to 10000 ms.

tools.name: request_user_input
tools.description: Request user input for one to three short questions and wait for the response. This tool is only available in Plan mode.

questions.description: Questions to show the user. Prefer 1 and do not exceed 3

header.description: Short header label shown in the UI (12 or fewer chars).

options.description: Provide 2-3 mutually exclusive choices. Put the recommended option first and suffix its label with "(Recommended)". Do not include an "Other" option in this list; the client will add a free-form "Other" option automatically.

description.description: One short sentence explaining impact/tradeoff if selected.

question.description: Single-sentence prompt shown to the user.

tools.name: clock
tools.description: Tools for reading and waiting on time.

tools.name: sleep
tools.description: Pause execution for a specified duration. The sleep ends early when new input arrives for the active turn. Returns the elapsed wall-clock time.

duration_ms.description: How long to sleep in milliseconds. Must be between 1 and 43200000.

tools.name: collaboration
tools.description: Tools for spawning and managing sub-agents.

tools.name: followup_task
tools.description: Send a follow-up task to an existing non-root target agent and trigger a turn if it is idle. If the target is already running, deliver the task promptly at message boundaries while sampling, or after the pending tool call completes.

message.description: Message text to send to the target agent.

target.description: Agent id or canonical task name to send a follow-up task to (from spawn_agent).

tools.name: interrupt_agent
tools.description: Interrupt an agent's current turn, if any, and return its previous status. The agent remains available for messages and follow-up tasks.

target.description: Agent id or canonical task name to interrupt (from spawn_agent).

tools.name: list_agents
tools.description: List live agents in the current root thread tree. Optionally filter by task-path prefix.

path_prefix.description: Task-path prefix filter without a trailing slash. Omit to list all live agents.

tools.name: send_message
tools.description: Send a message to an existing agent. The message will be delivered promptly. Does not trigger a new turn.

message.description: Message text to queue on the target agent.

target.description: Relative or canonical task name to message (from spawn_agent).

tools.name: spawn_agent
tools.description:
Available model overrides (optional; inherited parent model is preferred):
- `gpt-6.2-sol`: Fast, go-to model for coding and everyday work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority, ultrafast.
- `gpt-6.2-astra`: Our most capable model for complex coding and professional work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority, ultrafast.
- `gpt-6.1-terra`: Efficient model that excels at visual understanding and computer use. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6.1-sol`: Previous generation model for coding and everyday work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority, ultrafast.
- `gpt-6-astra`: Previous generation model for complex coding and professional work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority, ultrafast.
- `gpt-6-sol`: Legacy model for coding and everyday work. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6-luna`: Fast and affordable model for easier tasks. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-5.6-sol`: Legacy model for coding and everyday work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-5.6-terra`: Legacy balanced model for agentic coding. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-5.6-luna`: Legacy fast model for simpler tasks. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-5.5`: Legacy coding model. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh. Service tiers: priority.
        Spawns an agent to work on the specified task. If your current task is `/root/task1` and you spawn_agent with task_name "task_3" the agent will have canonical task name `/root/task1/task_3`.
You are then able to refer to this agent as `task_3` or `/root/task1/task_3` interchangeably. However an agent `/root/task2/task_3` would only be able to communicate with this agent via its canonical name `/root/task1/task_3`.
The spawned agent will have the same tools as you and the ability to spawn its own subagents.

It will be able to send you and other running agents messages, and its final answer will be provided to you when it finishes.
The new agent's canonical task name will be provided to it along with the message.

Note that passing `fork_turns="none"` will not pass any surrounding context to the spawned subagent, which may cause the agent to lack the context it needs to complete its task, whereas `fork_turns="all"` will provide the subagent with all surrounding context.

fork_turns.description: Parent history to inherit. Defaults to `all`; use `none` to start without parent history. Only `all` and `none` are supported.

message.description: Initial plain-text task for the new agent.

model.description: Model override for the new agent. Omit unless an explicit override is needed.

reasoning_effort.description: Reasoning effort override for the new agent. Omit to inherit the parent effort.

task_name.description: Task name for the new agent. Use lowercase letters, digits, and underscores.

tools.name: wait_agent
tools.description: Wait for a mailbox update from any live agent, including queued messages and final-status notifications. The wait also ends early when new user input is steered into the active turn. Does not return the content; returns either a summary of which agents have updates (if any), an interruption summary for steered input, or a timeout summary if no activity arrives before the deadline.

timeout_ms.description: Timeout in milliseconds. Defaults to 30000, min 10000, max 3600000.

tools.name: mcp__cua_repl
tools.description: UI automation through cua_repl using the initialized cua API.

tools.name: js
tools.description:
Control native apps or browsers on the user’s computer by reading or operating UI. Prefer purpose-built skills, connectors, APIs, or CLIs when available.

On the first invocation of `cua_repl`, or after resetting it, execute exactly one of the API calls shown below, optionally assigning its result to a variable. Do not add other API calls, waits, or snapshots to that invocation.
The tool result will include documentation and, when creating or selecting a tab or selecting an app, its initial UI state. Selecting a browser does not open a tab. Read that result before continuing.
Use only APIs described in the tool instructions or returned documentation.

When you need an inventory of available apps, browsers, and tabs, get a snapshot of all enabled surfaces. Otherwise, use the relevant entry point below:

```javascript
await cua.getState();
```

Use the first matching browser control option from the user's request:

For a tab @-mention (`mention=tab-v1`):
Pass the complete `plugin://...` URL to get the referenced tab.

```javascript
let tab = await cua.getTab({ mention: tabMentionUrl });
```

For an existing tab identified by URL in browser context (including the current IAB tab):

```javascript
let tab = await cua.getTab({ url }, { browser: browserId });
```

Known tab ID (`tabId` or `providerTabId`) and browser (name or browser @-mention):

```javascript
let tab = await cua.getTab(tabId, { browser: browserId });
```

To open a URL in the in-app browser (`@Browser`):

```javascript
let tab = await cua.createBrowserTab("iab", url, { visible: boolean });
```

To open a URL in another named browser: pass its name directly; do not call `getBrowser` first.

```javascript
let tab = await cua.createBrowserTab(browserName, url, browserOptions);
```

Known URL, only when the user has not specified a browser by name or @-mention:

```javascript
let browser = await cua.getBrowser({ url });
```

Browser IDs and options:

- `"mcpapps"`: use `cua.getBrowser({ id: "mcpapps" })` for existing full-screen MCP Apps in the task’s side panel.
- `"iab"` (in-app browser): in `createBrowserTab`, use `visible: true` to show the browser; `false` to keep it hidden.
- `"dot"` (Dot): use only when present in browser inventory. It accesses tabs on Dot's active main thread. `cua.getTab(tabId, { browser: "dot" })` selects an existing tab. `cua.createBrowserTab("dot", url, { visible: boolean })` creates one with the same visibility options as `"iab"`.
- `"chrome"` (@Chrome), `"edge"` (@Edge): pass a short, emoji-prefixed `sessionName` (e.g. `"🔎 Task"`) to `createBrowserTab` when starting a task.

If the user specifies an app to use, get the app by name, bundle ID, or path:

```javascript
let app = await cua.getApp("Example App");
```

To add other content to the tool result, use `nodeRepl.write(value)` for text or other values and `await nodeRepl.emitImage(image)` for images. The APIs listed above already display their documentation or UI state; do not wrap their results in `write` or `emitImage`.

If your context begins with a summary of an existing computer use task, call `await cua.rewriteDocumentation()` before continuing the computer use task to ensure you have a complete view of the necessary documentation.

Each `cua_repl.js` call opens or continues a browser activity. Keep consecutive calls together. The activity stays open across messages until you emit completion commentary.

**Manual takeover takes priority over the table below.** For a required manual browser step, call the documented takeover API before asking the user to act, unless takeover is already pending. Explain the required step in your final reply. Tab marking alone does not transfer control. While waiting for the user to finish and return control, emit no completion and make no CUA calls, even when answering side questions. The takeover API returning does not end this wait. When the user returns or unblocks you, resume browser work and apply the table. If they cancel, replace, or no longer need the browser work, close the activity before answering, even without another CUA call.

Completion is a standalone assistant commentary message containing only `::browser-complete{title="<headline>"}`. Never put it in a tool call or final reply. Use 3–6 words starting with a past-tense verb to describe the observed outcome. Omit identifiers.

After a user cancels pending browser work: commentary `::browser-complete{title="Stopped browser work"}`, then the final acknowledgement. No browser call is needed.

For an open browser activity:

| Next action                                   | Required output order                                                                     |
| --------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Another CUA call                              | Continue without completion.                                                              |
| A non-CUA tool, final reply, or chat question | Finish required tab marking, emit completion, then take that action in the same response. |

With no open activity, emit no completion. Later CUA use requires a fresh completion at the next table boundary.

If you need a one-time sign-in code, information, or confirmation from the user, follow the table and ask in chat. One-time code entry alone does not require takeover. This tool is part of plugin `unified-computer-use`.

code.description: JavaScript to execute using the initialized cua_repl runtime.

timeout_ms.description: Optional execution timeout in milliseconds. Defaults to 30000 (30 seconds) when omitted.

title.description: Short user-facing description of what this code block is doing. Prefer a few words in present-progressive form, such as 'Checking the mobile layout' or 'Comparing prices', over imperative or past-tense titles.

tools.name: js_reset
tools.description: Reset the persistent cua_repl JavaScript session. All JavaScript bindings are discarded. The next cua_repl.js call initializes a fresh runtime for the enabled surfaces. This does not close browser tabs or native apps, or erase their state. This tool is part of plugin `unified-computer-use`.

## Skills
A skill is a set of local instructions to follow that is stored in a `SKILL.md` file. Below is the list of skills that can be used. Each entry includes a name, description, and a short path that can be expanded into an absolute path using the skill roots table.
### Skill roots
- `r0` = `/Users/alexcallow/.agents/skills`
- `r1` = `/Users/alexcallow/.codex/skills/.system`
- `r2` = `/Users/alexcallow/.codex/plugins/cache/egm/egm/0.1.1/skills`
- `r3` = `/Users/alexcallow/.codex/plugins/cache/openai-bundled`
### Available skills
- imagegen: Generate or edit raster images when the task benefits from AI-created bitmap visuals such as photos, illustrations, textures, sprites, mockups, or transparent-background cutouts. Use when Codex should create a brand-new image, transform an existing image, or derive visual variants from references, and the output should be a bitmap asset rather than repo-native code or vector. Do not use when the task is better handled by editing existing SVG/vector/code-native assets, extending an established icon or logo system, or building the visual directly in HTML/CSS/canvas. (file: r1/imagegen/SKILL.md)
- openai-docs: API first-timers, Codex/Work Q&A. If the user already has an OpenAI API integration, skip this skill for API questions and use the developer docs. Read this skill before answering how Codex or ChatGPT Work behaves, where to find a feature, or how to configure or troubleshoot this app or coding agent. This includes conversation history, model and cache behavior, instruction precedence, permissions, and tool availability. Skip action requests, such as scheduling an automation, and tasks fully answered by supplied text or data. (file: r1/openai-docs/SKILL.md)

(file: r0/apollo-client/SKILL.md)
- built-in-browser: Read this skill before the first step that uses the built-in browser, the browser pane inside the Codex desktop app (also called the in-app browser, the browser pane, Codex's browser, or "your own browser"), whose tools are named mcp__Claude_Browser__* when the session runs in the desktop app and mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* when a cloud session is linked to the person's computer; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser tool instead. It is not for Codex in Chrome (mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use. (file: r0/synced/31fc0c17-6ddd-4792-886e-5cbd4fcd4b6f_1f3233f3-c0e3-424e-a407-80f78eb29aa1/built-in-browser/SKILL.md)
- chrome-browser: Read this skill before the first step that uses Codex in Chrome, the browser extension whose tools are named mcp__claude-in-chrome__* (also called Chrome, the browser extension, or the external browser) and which acts in the person's real Chrome with their own sign-ins; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__claude-in-chrome tool instead. ---
name: egm-zoom-out
description: Skeptical Architect persona focused on high-altitude simplicity, minimalism, YAGNI, and codebase reuse.
license: Apache-2.0
---

# Core Mandates (Universal Goldfish Context)

You are a specialized Goldfish subagent operating within the Elephant-Goldfish Model. You have been delegated a specific high-altitude task by the root agent (the Elephant).

1. **Strict Read-Only Protocol**: You are a strictly read-only agent. You have NO tools to modify the workspace, write files, or compile code. Do not attempt to fix or refactor any code.
2. **Stateless Mindset (Goldfish Isolation)**: You evaluate plans with zero conversational history or external assumptions. You must read the document as a naive team member or fresh reader who has just joined the project.
3. **No Chitchat**: Avoid conversational filler. Focus exclusively on technical rationale and findings. Do not narrate your tool usage.

---

# Role

You are **Skeptical Architect (Zoom Out Goldfish)**.
You are highly analytical, pragmatic, and focused on simplicity, minimalism, and long-term codebase health. You despise unnecessary complexity, premature optimizations, and speculative features ("YAGNI"). You constantly ask yourself:
* Are we building something we don't actually need right now?
* Are we over-engineering this solution?
* Are we missing existing utilities, services, or APIs that already solve this?
* Are we introducing architectural dead-ends?
* Are we getting lost in implementation-level details (weeds) rather than focusing on the high-level architecture?

Your job is to look at the big picture and enforce simplicity.

---

# Instructions

Inspect the `Mode` parameter specified by the caller:

### IF Mode: BRAINSTORM (Upstream Concept Ideation)
Evaluate the raw feature concept from a high-altitude Contrarian / YAGNI perspective:
1. **YAGNI Assessment**: Does this feature actually need to exist right now? Can an existing library, API, or service solve 90% of the problem without writing new code?
2. **Codebase Reuse**: Perform codebase searches to identify existing components that could fulfill the feature's intent.
3. Report complexity risks and reuse opportunities back to the orchestrator.

### IF Mode: REVIEW (Document Audit)
Audit the target document file specified by the caller:

1. **Enforce Zoom-Out Standard**: Evaluate the target scope against the **Zoom-Out Standard** (`resources/document_standards/zoom-out-standard.md`). Check for context sufficiency, root problem focus, simplicity, anti-weeds, and leveraging existing solutions.
2. **Verify Reuse with Code Search**: When a design proposes new utilities, modules, classes, or helper functions, you **MUST** perform code searches in the codebase to verify whether equivalent or similar components already exist. If matches are found, suggest reuse instead of writing new code.
3. **Check for Premature Details**: Flag any parts of the design or plan that get bogged down in low-level code implementation details (e.g., concrete helper functions, loop variables, minor variables) rather than focusing on architectural interfaces, data flow, and components.
4. **Confirm Root Problem Focus**: Ensure that the proposed design directly addresses the root problem. If it merely patches a symptom or diverges from the project's core philosophy, flag it.

### Audit Vectors:
* **Context Insufficiency**: The document lacks enough context to understand the high-level objective and motivation.
* **YAGNI Violations**: Proposing features, abstractions, configurations, or interfaces designed for future, speculative requirements.
* **Reinventing the Wheel**: Proposing new utilities or components when existing ones can be reused. Use code search to investigate.
* **Premature Optimizations**: Proposing caching, database partitioning, asynchronous processing, or background queues without proven performance bottlenecks.
* **Altitude Drops (Weeds)**: Writing detailed pseudocode or listing minor implementation helper functions instead of high-level structure.
* **Architectural Dead-Ends**: Proposing coupling or designs that block future expansion, or implementing a speculative interface now to avoid it.

---

# Output Format

Report your findings back to the orchestrator in plain, natural language.

#### IF Mode: REVIEW
For each finding, include:
1. **Severity**: [Blocker | Major | Nit]
2. **Affected Scope**: Section heading or line numbers.
3. **Simplicity Rationale**: Clear reasoning on why the proposal is over-engineered or violates YAGNI.

#### IF Mode: BRAINSTORM
For each concept risk or reuse opportunity, include:
1. **Severity**: [Blocker | Major | Nit]
2. **Dimension**: Contrarian / YAGNI & Code Minimization
3. **Challenge/Risk**: Why this feature/complexity might be unnecessary or replaceable.
4. **Alternative / Reuse Opportunity**: Existing codebase API/library or simpler alternative.
# Zoom Out Standard

This standard defines the quality bar for evaluating high-level designs,
architectures, and implementation plans from a high-altitude perspective.

## Core Principle

A design passes if it solves the root problem in the simplest possible way,
leverages existing infrastructure and codebase conventions, avoids premature
optimization or speculative features (YAGNI), and maintains appropriate
abstraction boundaries without getting bogged down in low-level code
implementation details.

## 0. Context Sufficiency (Prerequisite Check)

*   **Understanding the Objective**: The document must contain enough
    information to define the overall objective. If the reviewer cannot
    determine *what* we are trying to achieve and *why*, the review must fail
    immediately with a request for context.

## 1. Root Problem Focus

*   **Symptom vs. Root Cause**: The design must solve the underlying problem,
    not just apply a local band-aid to symptoms.
*   **Project Alignment**: The design must align with the high-level goals and
    architectural philosophy defined in the project's root documentation
    (`README.md` or `context.md`).

## 2. Simplicity & Extensibility

*   **YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It)**: Reject abstractions, code paths, or
    features built solely for speculative future requirements.
*   **Premature Optimization**: Avoid introducing complexity (caching, sharding,
    async queues) before performance bottlenecks are proven.
*   **Minimalist Data Flow**: Ensure data passes through the minimal number of
    components.
*   **No Architectural Dead-Ends**: Use clean interfaces and boundaries to allow
    future expansion without blocking it, without implementing speculative
    features now.

## 3. Anti-Weeds (Altitude Control)

*   **Premature Detail**: High-level sections must focus on architecture,
    interfaces, and data flows, not code-level implementation details (e.g.,
    helper functions or loop variables).
*   **Workarounds vs. Structural Fixes**: Avoid complex local workarounds;
    propose changes to the root component if that is cleaner.
*   **Right Placement (Architectural Fit)**: Ensure new logic is placed in the
    correct layer/component according to separation of concerns.

## 4. Leverage Existing

*   **Codebase Reuse**: Search the codebase and reuse existing utilities,
    classes, or modules instead of reinventing them. Ensure the candidate for
    reuse is stable, maintained, and does not violate dependency boundaries.
*   **Pattern Consistency**: Follow established design patterns in the codebase.
*   **Platform Standards**: Use established ecosystem frameworks and standard libraries
    instead of bespoke or ad-hoc custom solutions.
*   **Identify Anti-Patterns**: Actively flag known anti-patterns
    (e.g., bypassing standard authentication, hardcoding deployment configurations).

     1	# Bulk CSV inventory import
     2	
     3	- **Author** — Alex Callow
     4	- **Status** — Proposed
     5	- **Date** — 2026-11-26
     6	
     7	## Overview
     8	
     9	Inventory operators can upload `inventory_frame.csv` from the running application and see the result as the job progresses. A routine update changes only the frames named in the file. An authoritative snapshot can also retire missing frames within a declared area of the inventory. Every accepted change is visible in frame history.
    10	
    11	## The Problem
    12	
    13	The application supports individual frame edits, but operators receive inventory updates as CSV files. Applying a file by hand is slow and makes it difficult to identify which rows failed. An older export can also conflict with a newer edit or omit frames that were created after the export. Operators need to apply the file, see what was accepted or skipped, and understand why a frame changed.
    14	
    15	## Goals
    16	
    17	- Let an authorized operator upload the supplied 45-field CSV from the application and see job progress, final counts, and actionable row errors.
    18	- Apply `DELTA` by default. Leave absent frames alone, preserve newer edits unless the operator explicitly forces a conflicting change, and avoid duplicate frame versions and events on retry or re-upload of unchanged rows.
    19	- Support `FULL_SNAPSHOT` for a single declared scope. Require country and region for environment-level scopes. Protect frames present in malformed rows, frames changed after the export watermark, and partitions with newer snapshots. Prevent retirement when the malformed-row rate exceeds 5% and abort before inventory writes if more than 10% of scoped active frames would retire.
    20	- Preserve accepted versions, source timestamps, and import lineage so operators can trace updates, forced corrections, and retirements.
    21	
    22	## Non-Goals
    23	
    24	- Hard deletion of inventory during import.
    25	- Arbitrary CSV schemas, field mapping, or automatic repair of malformed values.
    26	- A single snapshot covering several separately named scopes in the first release. Operators can submit separate regional snapshots or use `DELTA` for a cross-region update.
    27	
    28	## Technical Plan (Architecture)
    29	
    30	### Upload and dispatch
    31	
    32	```text
    33	Operator → web app → BFF → Spring Boot → import_jobs
    34	Operator → presigned PUT → S3 → SQS standard queue → Spring Boot → Temporal
    35	                                   SQS retries → DLQ → dispatch reconciler
    36	Temporal worker → pinned S3 object → PostgreSQL staging → inventory apply
    37	Inventory apply → frame versions + job outcome
    38	Operator ← web app ← BFF ← Spring Boot job status and row errors
    39	```
    40	
    41	The job creation API takes the import mode, optional snapshot scope and export watermark, and explicit force flag. Spring Boot validates the requested scope and permissions, creates an AWAITING_UPLOAD job, and returns its ID and the presigned PUT details through the BFF. The upload key is uploads/{jobId}/inventory_frame.csv. Use a create-only PUT and persist the accepted S3 object version so all retries read the same bytes. Expose job status, counts, fatal errors, and paginated row errors through the BFF.
    42	
    43	Configure S3 to send object-created notifications for the uploads/ prefix directly to a standard SQS queue in the same AWS Region. Grant the bucket permission to publish through a queue policy scoped to the bucket ARN and owner account. The Spring Boot consumer handles the native S3 notification envelope, recognizes the S3 test event, and processes each object record. It decodes the key and verifies the bucket, key, object version, and size, then conditionally records PENDING and starts Temporal workflow csv-import-{jobId}. Duplicate or out-of-order records must preserve the existing object binding and job state. Acknowledge the message after each applicable record has been handled, including confirming successful or already-completed workflow dispatch. If processing a later record fails, replay of earlier records uses the same job and workflow identities. Retry with backoff. Before a DLQ event can fail a job, reconcile ambiguous workflow starts and check that the job is still dispatchable. Reconcile old AWAITING_UPLOAD and PENDING jobs against S3 and Temporal.
    44	
    45	### Staging and validation
    46	
    47	Accept files up to 10 MiB and 10,000 data rows, whichever limit is reached first. Verify object size before dispatch and enforce both limits while streaming. The header does not count. Exceeding either limit fails the job before inventory writes. Keep uploaded object versions and row diagnostics for 7 days. Keep the minimal durable job outcome and import lineage available to history after diagnostics expire. Bound retries and reconciliation within the object retention period.
    48	
    49	Interpret the CSV created_date and modified_date fields as UTC at their supplied precision. Use UTC for source_modified_at storage and explicitly interpret the existing offset-free PostgreSQL column as UTC regardless of the database session timezone. Convert source timestamps to instants for watermark and manual-edit comparisons.
    50	
    51	The Temporal worker reads the pinned object and streams logical CSV records into job- and attempt-scoped UNLOGGED staging. Heartbeats report progress and let the worker detect cancellation. Keep the EOF completion marker in the same unlogged storage as the data. Before apply, check the marker and staged counts. If a crash leaves staging incomplete or empty, reload from S3. Store row errors with stable job, row, and error keys for retries. Track identifiable frame IDs independently of row validity. Hash canonical typed frame values with SHA-256 over a versioned, ordered encoding. Preserve meaningful text, normalize typed numeric values by value, encode null distinctly, order external references by type, and preserve the position of links. Exclude job metadata, version validity, and source timestamps from the payload hash. Compare hashes using the same encoding version. After staging, reject every row for a frame ID that appears more than once, report DUPLICATE_FRAME_ID for each duplicate row, and keep the ID in the snapshot presence set. Count each rejected logical record once toward the malformed-row threshold, even if it has several validation errors.
    52	
    53	### Inventory and history
    54	
    55	Use the existing frame table for stable identity and frame_version for current and historical values. Resolve region, town, postcode, and format through existing lookup tables. Attach external references and ordered links to the resulting frame version. Add job, row error, scope watermark, and import lineage storage through Flyway. Map the complete CSV to the existing model, including site and spec fields on frame_version. The BFF, protobuf service definitions, Spring service, and worker need changes for job creation, progress, and application.
    56	
    57	Re-read the current version under the existing stable-frame lock. A newer source timestamp creates a version. Equal timestamp and hash is a no-op. Skip and report stale rows and same-timestamp collisions unless forceOverwrite is authorized and set, and record both hashes for collisions. Manual writes set source_modified_at from database statement time after locking, and CSV writes preserve the input timestamp. For existing manual versions that inherited their source timestamp, use the version’s valid_from as the effective conflict baseline. Identify those versions at migration time and preserve the original source_modified_at for history. Forced corrections record FORCED_OVERWRITE and import_job_id. Subsequent imports compare against the current version’s source timestamp, including when a forced overwrite moves that timestamp backward. For example, an 11:00 row is newer after a forced overwrite replaces a 12:00 version with a 10:00 version. Use the same database-generated boundary for closing and opening a version, strictly later than the previous valid_from.
    58	
    59	When a frame has no current version and its latest version was closed by MANUAL_DELETE, require an authorized forceOverwrite to restore it in either import mode. Without that flag, skip the row and record MANUALLY_DELETED in the job’s row errors. With it, append a new current version, preserve the CSV source timestamp, and record FORCED_OVERWRITE and import_job_id in the apply transaction. Compare and restore under the stable-frame lock.
    60	
    61	Promote a complete staging attempt in one transaction. Acquire the job lock and verify eligibility before writing. Use one source candidate per target key and MERGE RETURNING where it fits. Close current versions and append replacements in separate set-based statements. Commit inventory, versioned references and links, the applicable scope watermark, and job result together. If the worker loses the commit response, return the stored result when it retries.
    62	
    63	### Snapshot apply
    64	
    65	Keep staging outside the inventory lock. During promotion, take a shared transaction-scoped inventory lock for manual writes and DELTA and an exclusive lock for FULL_SNAPSHOT. Obtain frame locks in stable ID order. Evaluate scope membership, watermark checks, and retirement against the protected pre-apply view.
    66	
    67	Require scope to be GLOBAL or a canonical country, country/region, or country/region/environment path. Use the explicit snapshot_as_of where available, otherwise derive it from MAX(modified_date) on the complete file. Check freshness and reject watermarks below the greatest committed value for the scope or its ancestors. A broader snapshot can still apply its present rows under the ordinary conflict rules when a descendant has a newer watermark. Protect that entire descendant subtree from retirement.
    68	
    69	Before writing inventory, fail the entire snapshot for a header-only file, an incomplete export, or an unrecoverable CSV parse error. Also fail the snapshot if any row has no recoverable frame ID or any record is outside the declared scope. Keep job diagnostics and leave inventory and the scope watermark unchanged. Count any identifiable frame ID in the CSV as present, including when other fields are malformed. Among absent active frames, exclude protected child scopes and current versions whose valid_from or source_modified_at exceeds the export watermark. Record SKIPPED_RETIREMENT_NEWER_THAN_SNAPSHOT for the latter. If eligible retirements exceed 10% of all active frames in the declared scope, fail before inventory writes. If more than 5% of CSV rows are malformed, fail the entire snapshot before writing inventory. Keep the job diagnostics and leave the scope watermark unadvanced. Represent each accepted retirement with a new RETIRED version and MISSING_FROM_FULL_SNAPSHOT. Advance only the incoming scope watermark on a successful commit.
    70	
    71	Exclude snapshot-retired frames from the default inventory list. Expose them through an explicit retired filter, direct lookup, and frame history.
    72	
    73	A FULL_SNAPSHOT can reactivate an unchanged row when the current version was retired with MISSING_FROM_FULL_SNAPSHOT, the incoming export watermark is strictly later than that retirement version’s valid_from, and the row’s source timestamp and canonical payload hash match the last live version. Append a new live version in the apply transaction. Apply normal conflict rules to other rows and to DELTA imports.
    74	
    75	## Alternatives Considered
    76	
    77	### Forward S3 notifications through Lambda
    78	
    79	A Lambda bridge can normalize events or route them to several destinations. The import has a single queue, and Spring Boot can consume the native event. The bridge adds a deployment and another delivery failure path.
    80	
    81	**Rejected by author** — Send S3 notifications directly to the standard SQS queue to remove the forwarding hop.
    82	
    83	### Use logged staging
    84	
    85	Logged staging can survive a PostgreSQL restart or failover and avoids downloading and parsing the same object again after staging is lost. It adds write-ahead logging and storage work for intermediate rows. The initial design uses UNLOGGED staging with replay from the pinned S3 object. Measure the cost of both approaches at the maximum supported upload size before committing to larger files.
    86	
    87	### Migrate to the six-table inventory model and separate frame history
    88	
    89	Separate site and spec entities would give those concepts independent identities and lifecycles. A migration would also change existing inventory reads and writes and would need to preserve historical values when site or spec records change.
    90	
    91	**Rejected by author** — Extend the existing versioned schema for this release. It already gives current and historical frames one authoritative store and preserves links and external references per version. A separate history store would add a second representation of those changes.
    92	
    93	## Detailed Implementation Plan
    94	
    95	Deliver the operator-facing DELTA path first. Enable FULL_SNAPSHOT after measuring transaction duration and verifying retirement safeguards against the supplied CSV and concurrent writers.
    96	
    97	1. Add the import storage and schema invariants.
    98	
    99	   - Create [V3__create_inventory_import.sql](../../src/backend/src/main/resources/db/migration/V3__create_inventory_import.sql) for import_jobs, import_row_errors, staging rows and completion markers, scope watermarks, and import provenance on frame versions. Enforce one accepted object version per job, valid scope shape, and stable row error keys. Keep staging rows and their completion marker unlogged, with indexes for job/attempt and presence checks. Keep the durable job result separate.
   100	   - Update [frame-inventory-schema.md](../../docs/frame-inventory-schema/frame-inventory-schema.md) to document source timestamps, interval boundaries, collision handling, retirement, and force-only restoration after manual deletion.
   101	
   102	2. Add the backend job and worker entry points.
   103	
   104	   Backend Java paths below are relative to [src/backend/src/main/java/com/global/ct/frameinventory](../../src/backend/src/main/java/com/global/ct/frameinventory).
   105	
   106	   - Modify [build.gradle](../../src/backend/build.gradle) for the AWS, Temporal, and CSV parsing dependencies. This standard defines the quality bar for evaluating high-level designs,
architectures, and implementation plans from a high-altitude perspective.

## Core Principle

A design passes if it solves the root problem in the simplest possible way,
leverages existing infrastructure and codebase conventions, avoids premature
optimization or speculative features (YAGNI), and maintains appropriate
abstraction boundaries without getting bogged down in low-level code

## 0. Context Sufficiency (Prerequisite Check)

*   **No Architectural Dead-Ends**: Use clean interfaces and boundaries to allow

*   **Platform Standards**: Use established ecosystem frameworks and standard libraries

     2	
     3	- **Author** — Alex Callow
     4	- **Status** — Proposed
     5	- **Date** — 2026-11-26
     6	
     7	## Overview
     8	
     9	Inventory operators can upload `inventory_frame.csv` from the running application and see the result as the job progresses. A routine update changes only the frames named in the file. An authoritative snapshot can also retire missing frames within a declared area of the inventory. Every accepted change is visible in frame history.
    10	
    11	## The Problem
    12	
    13	The application supports individual frame edits, but operators receive inventory updates as CSV files. Applying a file by hand is slow and makes it difficult to identify which rows failed. An older export can also conflict with a newer edit or omit frames that were created after the export. Operators need to apply the file, see what was accepted or skipped, and understand why a frame changed.
    14	
    15	## Goals
    16	
    17	- Let an authorized operator upload the supplied 45-field CSV from the application and see job progress, final counts, and actionable row errors.
    18	- Apply `DELTA` by default. Leave absent frames alone, preserve newer edits unless the operator explicitly forces a conflicting change, and avoid duplicate frame versions and events on retry or re-upload of unchanged rows.
    19	- Support `FULL_SNAPSHOT` for a single declared scope. Require country and region for environment-level scopes. Protect frames present in malformed rows, frames changed after the export watermark, and partitions with newer snapshots. Prevent retirement when the malformed-row rate exceeds 5% and abort before inventory writes if more than 10% of scoped active frames would retire.
    20	- Preserve accepted versions, source timestamps, and import lineage so operators can trace updates, forced corrections, and retirements.
    21	
    22	## Non-Goals
    23	
    24	- Hard deletion of inventory during import.
    25	- Arbitrary CSV schemas, field mapping, or automatic repair of malformed values.
    26	- A single snapshot covering several separately named scopes in the first release. Operators can submit separate regional snapshots or use `DELTA` for a cross-region update.
    27

    31

    33	Operator → web app → BFF → Spring Boot → import_jobs
    34	Operator → presigned PUT → S3 → SQS standard queue → Spring Boot → Temporal

    38	Operator ← web app ← BFF ← Spring Boot job status and row errors

The upload key is uploads/{jobId}/inventory_frame.csv. Use a create-only PUT and persist the accepted S3 object version so all retries read the same bytes. FILE 0 INSTRUCTIONS.md
# Frame Inventory — Exercise Instructions

## 1. Scenario

In the **out-of-home (OOH) media** industry, advertisers buy time on physical
display surfaces such as roadside billboards, transport platforms, mall
screens, and bus shelters. Each surface is referred to as a **frame**, and an
operator's catalogue of frames — including their location, size, format,
status, and commercial attributes — is collectively known as the **frame
inventory**. Keeping that inventory accurate matters: every downstream process
(planning, pricing, booking, reporting) depends on it.

For this exercise the candidate will build a small but realistic service for
managing OOH frame inventory. Scoping is part of the exercise: the candidate
is not expected to deliver every feature one could imagine, but to pick a
meaningful subset and deliver it well.

## 2. What we provide

This repository is the starting point. It is intentionally minimal so the
candidate can make their own architectural choices, but it includes enough
infrastructure to skip the boilerplate and start delivering business value
straight away.

| Path                  | Contents                                                                          |
| --------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `src/backend/`        | Bare Spring Boot 3.5 + Java 21 module (Gradle). Exposes only `/api/health`.       |
| `src/frontend/`       | Next.js + React 19 + TypeScript module that calls the backend `/api/health` on boot. |
| `docker-compose.yml`  | One-command infra: backend, frontend, MongoDB, Postgres, OpenSearch + Dashboards.  |
| `data/`               | Extract from the legacy system — `inventory_frame.csv` (~1.3k OOH frame rows).    |
| `design-system/`      | Design system the frontend must be built against — components, tokens, guidance.  |
| `README.md`           | How to run the stack locally, ports, and credentials for the bundled services.    |

> **A note on the suggested infrastructure.** The `docker-compose.yml` file
> is a starting point, not a requirement. The candidate is free to swap any
> of these services for tooling they prefer (a different database, search
> engine, message broker, hosting model, etc.) as long as the final stack
> still runs end-to-end with a single command. If the candidate does choose
> to use the services provided here, they should pick **one** of the two
> datastores for their domain data — either `mongodb` *or* `postgres`,
> not both — and remove the service they don't need (along with its volume)
> so the stack reflects the design actually built.

In addition, the candidate receives:

- A **provisioned OpenAI Codex API key**. Use of an AI coding assistant is
  explicitly expected — we want to see how the candidate collaborates with a
  model, not whether they can hand-write every line.

## 3. Features

The candidate should deliver the following features:

1. **Add a frame.** A user can create a new frame through the application and
   see it persisted in the inventory.
2. **Edit a frame.** A user can amend an existing frame's attributes and have
   the changes saved.
3. **Bulk upload frames from a CSV.** A user can upload a CSV through the
   application and have the rows ingested into the inventory. The supplied
   `data/inventory_frame.csv` is the file to validate this feature
   against. This is a user-driven feature of the running app, not a one-off
   bootstrap step.
4. **View a frame's history.** A user can see the audit trail of changes to
   any given frame.

How these features are surfaced, structured, and tested is left to the
candidate's judgement.

## 4. Domain data

The shape of a frame is anchored by the legacy export shipped at
`data/inventory_frame.csv` (~1,300 rows) and by the prototype in
`design-system/`. The candidate is expected to inspect both and design a
domain model they are comfortable defending.

At a high level, each frame in the export carries:

- **Identity** — a frame identifier, plus references to downstream systems
  (Broadsign, pricing, linked frames).
- **Location** — country, region, town, postcode, latitude/longitude,
  address, and distance to the nearest school.
- **Site & position** — the kind of place the frame lives in (station,
  underground, roadside, airport, etc.) and where on that site it sits.
- **Format** — classic vs digital, format code, dimensions / pixels /
  aspect ratio, illumination, number of slots, size grouping.
- **Lifecycle** — created/modified timestamps, status, and a status reason.
- **Commercials** — impact weight, pricing grade, production rate card,
  premium flag.

The legacy column names and groupings are not prescriptive — the candidate
should design the domain model that best fits the features in §3, and
document the assumptions they made along the way.

## 5. Additional Requirements

Install and use the **[Entire CLI](https://entire.io)**. Entire hooks into the
candidate's git workflow and, on every push, captures the Codex agent
sessions that produced the changes and links them to the corresponding
commits as *checkpoints*. The result is a searchable record of how the
solution was actually built: the prompts used, the iterations the candidate
went through, the suggestions they accepted, and — just as important — the
ones they rejected or refined.

This is not about surveillance; it is about giving us a fair signal of
**how** the candidate works with AI tooling. We are far less interested in
whether code came from a human keystroke or a model completion than in
whether the candidate exercised judgement, scoped well, and reviewed the
output critically.

> **Note:** Codex support in Entire is currently in preview. The candidate
> should follow Entire's setup documentation for the latest supported
> workflow.

## 6. Submission

When the candidate is ready, they should share a **public GitHub repository**
containing their solution. The repository must include:

- All source code and anything else required to run the solution.
- A README explaining how to run it, the design decisions taken, and the
  trade-offs made.
- The Entire **checkpoints branch** with the captured Codex sessions linked
  to commits, so we can review the AI collaboration alongside the code.

There is no fixed deadline; we recommend timeboxing the exercise to a few
focused sessions rather than open-ended work. If something blocks progress,
note it in the README rather than over-investing time on it.

Introduction
Section titled “Introduction”
When you’re developing cloud and serverless applications, you need to grant access to various AWS resources like S3 buckets and RDS databases.
To handle this, you create IAM roles and assign permissions through policies.
However, configuring these policies can be challenging, especially if you want to ensure minimal access of all principals to your resources.
LocalStack IAM Policy Stream automates the generation of IAM policies for your AWS API requests on your local machine.
This stream helps you identify the necessary permissions for your cloud application and allows you to detect logical errors, such as unexpected actions in your policies.
This tutorial will guide you through setting up IAM Policy Stream for a locally running AWS application.
We’ll use a basic example involving an S3 bucket, an SQS queue, and a bucket notification configuration.
You’ll generate the policy for the bucket notification configuration and insert it into the SQS queue.
Why use IAM Policy Stream?
Section titled “Why use IAM Policy Stream?”
LocalStack enables you to create and enforce local IAM roles and policies using the ENFORCE_IAM feature.
However, users often struggle to figure out the necessary permissions for different actions.
It’s important to find a balance, avoiding giving too many permissions while making sure the right ones are granted.
This challenge becomes more complex when dealing with AWS services that make requests not directly visible to users.
For instance, if an SNS topic sends a message to an SQS queue and the underlying call fails, there might be no clear error message, causing confusion, especially for those less familiar with the services.
IAM Policy Stream simplifies this by automatically generating the needed policies and showing them to users.
This makes it easier to integrate with resources, roles, and users, streamlining the development process.
Additionally, it serves as a useful learning tool, helping users understand the permissions linked to various AWS calls and improving the onboarding experience for newcomers to AWS.

Tutorial: Configure an S3 bucket for event notifications using SQS
Section titled “Tutorial: Configure an S3 bucket for event notifications using SQS”
In this tutorial, you will configure a LocalStack S3 bucket to send event notifications to an SQS queue.
You will then use IAM Policy Stream to generate the necessary IAM policy for the SQS queue.
You will use Terraform to create the resources and the AWS CLI to interact with them.
With LocalStack’s IAM enforcement enabled, you can thoroughly test your policy and ensure that the development setup mirrors the production environment.
Start your LocalStack container
Section titled “Start your LocalStack container”
Launch the LocalStack container on your local machine using the specified command:
Terminal window
LOCALSTACK_DEBUG=1 LOCALSTACK_IAM_SOFT_MODE=1 lstk start
In the above command:
LOCALSTACK_DEBUG=1 turns on detailed logging to check API calls and IAM violations.
LOCALSTACK_IAM_SOFT_MODE=1 lets you test IAM enforcement by logging violations without stopping the API calls.
Create the Terraform configuration
Section titled “Create the Terraform configuration”
Create a new file called main.tf for the Terraform setup of an S3 bucket and an SQS queue.
Start by using the aws_sqs_queue resource to create an SQS queue named s3-event-notification-queue.
resource "aws_sqs_queue" "queue" {
name = "s3-event-notification-queue"
}
Next, use the aws_s3_bucket resource to create an S3 bucket called s3-event-notification-bucket.
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "bucket" {
bucket = "s3-event-notification-bucket"
}
Finally, use the aws_s3_bucket_notification resource to link the S3 bucket with the SQS queue for sending notifications:
resource "aws_s3_bucket_notification" "bucket_notification" {
bucket = aws_s3_bucket.bucket.id
queue {
queue_arn = aws_sqs_queue.queue.arn
events = ["s3:ObjectCreated:*"]
}
}
Deploy the Terraform configuration
Section titled “Deploy the Terraform configuration”
You can use lstk terraform to deploy your Terraform configuration within the LocalStack environment.
Run the following commands to initialize and apply the Terraform configuration:
Terminal window
lstk terraform init
lstk terraform apply
You will be prompted to confirm the changes.
Type yes to continue.
Since LocalStack is used, no real AWS resources are created.
LocalStack will emulate ephemeral development resources that will be removed automatically once you stop the LocalStack container.
After applying the Terraform configuration, the output will appear similar to this:

Start the IAM Policy Stream
Section titled “Start the IAM Policy Stream”
Access the LocalStack Web Application and go to the IAM Policy Stream dashboard.
This feature enables you to directly examine the generated policies, displaying the precise permissions required for each API call.
You’ll observe the Stream active status icon, indicating that making any local AWS API request will trigger the generation of an IAM Policy.
Now, let’s proceed to upload a file to the S3 bucket to trigger the event notification and generate the IAM policy.
Trigger the event notification
Section titled “Trigger the event notification”
Create a new file named some-log-file.log and upload it to the S3 bucket using the AWS CLI:

lstk aws s3 cp some-log-file.log s3://s3-event-notification-bucket/
Uploading a file will activate an event notification, sending a message to the SQS queue.
However, since the SQS queue lacks the necessary permissions, an IAM violation will appear in the IAM Policy Stream dashboard.

Generate the IAM policy
Section titled “Generate the IAM policy”
Go to the IAM Policy Stream dashboard and review the API calls such as PutObject, SendMessage, and ReceiveMessage.
Notice that the SendMessage call was denied due to an IAM violation.
Click on the SQS.SendMessage action to see the suggested IAM policy.
LocalStack automatically recommends a resource-based policy for the SQS queue arn:aws:sqs:us-east-1:000000000000:s3-event-notification-queue.
Copy this policy and incorporate it into your Terraform configuration under the aws_sqs_queue resource by adding the policy attribute:
resource "aws_sqs_queue" "queue" {
name = "s3-event-notification-queue"
policy = <<POLICY
{
"Version": "2012-10-17",
"Statement": [
{
"Sid": "Test22bf6867",
"Effect": "Allow",
"Action": "sqs:SendMessage",
"Resource": "arn:aws:sqs:us-east-1:000000000000:s3-event-notification-queue",
"Principal": {
"Service": [
"s3.amazonaws.com"
]
},
"Condition": {
"ArnEquals": {
"aws:SourceArn": "arn:aws:s3:::s3-event-notification-bucket"
}
}
}
]
}
POLICY
}

Generate a comprehensive policy
Section titled “Generate a comprehensive policy”
In scenarios where there are many AWS services, and every AWS API request generates a policy it might be cumbersome to analyze every policy.
In such cases, you can generate one comprehensive policy for all your AWS resources together.
You can navigate to the Summary Policy tab on the IAM Policy Stream dashboard.
This concatenates the policy per principle which the policy should be attached to.
For the example above, you would be able to see the Identity Policy for the root user which has all the actions and resources inside one single policy file for the operations we performed.
On the other hand, you have the Resource Policy for the SQS queue, where you can see the permission necessary for the subscription.
For larger AWS applications, you would be able to find multiple roles and multiple resource-based policies depending on your scenario.

Conclusion
Section titled “Conclusion”
IAM Policy Stream streamlines your development process by minimizing the manual creation of policies and confirming the necessity of granted permissions.
However, it is advisable to manually confirm that your policy aligns with your intended actions.
Your code may unintentionally make requests, and LocalStack considers all requests made during policy generation as valid.
A practical scenario is automating tests, such as integration or end-to-end testing, against your application using LocalStack.
This setup allows LocalStack to automatically generate policies with the required permissions.
However, it’s important to note that these generated policies may not cover all possible requests, as only the requests made during testing are included.
You can then review and customize the policies to meet your needs, ensuring that overly permissive policies don’t find their way into production environment

syntax = "proto3";

package frameinventory.v1;

option java_package = "com.global.ct.frameinventory.grpc.v1";
option java_multiple_files = true;
option java_outer_classname = "FramesProto";

import "google/protobuf/empty.proto";
import "google/protobuf/timestamp.proto";

service FrameManagement {
  rpc ListFrames(ListFramesRequest) returns (ListFramesResponse);
  rpc GetFrame(GetFrameRequest) returns (Frame);
  rpc GetFrameHistory(GetFrameHistoryRequest) returns (GetFrameHistoryResponse);
  rpc CreateFrame(CreateFrameRequest) returns (Frame);
  rpc UpdateFrame(UpdateFrameRequest) returns (Frame);
  rpc DeleteFrame(DeleteFrameRequest) returns (google.protobuf.Empty);
}

message ListFramesRequest {
  // Zero-based page. Defaults to 0.
  optional int32 page = 1;
  // Defaults to 25. Valid values are 1 through 50.
  optional int32 size = 2;
}

message ListFramesResponse {
  repeated Frame items = 1;
  int32 page = 2;
  int32 size = 3;
  bool has_next = 4;
}

message GetFrameRequest {
  string frame_id = 1;
}

message GetFrameHistoryRequest {
  string frame_id = 1;
}

message GetFrameHistoryResponse {
  // Newest first, with version ID descending as a tie break.
  repeated Frame versions = 1;
}

message CreateFrameRequest {
  // A case-sensitive identifier that can be used only once.
  string frame_id = 1;
  FrameData attributes = 2;
}

message UpdateFrameRequest {
  string frame_id = 1;
  // Must match the current version.
  int64 expected_version_id = 2;
  // Replaces writable attributes. Omitted optional fields are cleared.
  FrameData attributes = 3;
}

message DeleteFrameRequest {
  string frame_id = 1;
  // If absent the delete applies to the current version.
  optional int64 expected_version_id = 2;
}

message Frame {
  string frame_id = 1;
  int64 version_id = 2;
  google.protobuf.Timestamp valid_from = 3;
  google.protobuf.Timestamp valid_to = 4;
  bool current = 5;
  optional string change_source = 6;
  optional string closed_by_change_source = 7;
  // Local source timestamps in ISO 8601 format without an offset.
  optional string source_created_at = 8;
  optional string source_modified_at = 9;
  FrameData attributes = 10;
  map<string, string> external_references = 11;
  repeated string linked_frame_ids = 12;
}

message FrameData {
  // Manual writes accept LIVE, PENDING, MAINTENANCE, BLOCKED, or DRAFT.
  string status = 1;
  optional string status_reason = 2;
  optional string site_no = 3;
  optional string inventory_site_no = 4;
  optional string panel_number = 5;
  optional string location_id = 6;
  optional string environment = 7;
  optional string address = 8;
  optional string station = 9;
  optional string airport = 10;
  // Decimal strings retain PostgreSQL numeric precision.
  optional string latitude = 11;
  optional string longitude = 12;
  optional int32 distance_to_closest_school = 13;
  FrameLocation location = 14;
  FrameFormat format = 15;
  optional string size_code = 16;
  optional string aspect_ratio_code = 17;
  optional string t_size = 18;
  optional int32 pixel_height = 19;
  optional int32 pixel_width = 20;
  optional int32 illumination_type_id = 21;
  optional int32 number_of_slots = 22;
  optional string impact_weight = 23;
  bool premium = 24;
  optional string production_rate_card = 25;
  optional string production_rate_card_legacy = 26;
  optional string pricing_grade = 27;
}

message FrameLocation {
  string country_code = 1;
  string region = 2;
  string town = 3;
  string postcode = 4;
}

message FrameFormat {
  // Manual writes accept CLASSIC or DIGITAL.
  string technology = 1;
  string format_code = 2;
  string size_group_code = 3;
}

import { GraphQLError } from 'graphql'
import { GRAPHQL_ERROR_CODES } from '../consts'
import { callFrameRpc, type FrameClient } from '../frame-client'
import type { FrameData } from '../generated/frameinventory/v1/FrameData'
import type { Timestamp__Output } from '../generated/google/protobuf/Timestamp'
import type { FrameAttributesInput, Resolvers } from '../generated/graphql'

const MAX_VERSION_ID = 9_223_372_036_854_775_807n

function badInput(message: string) {
  return new GraphQLError(message, {
    extensions: { code: GRAPHQL_ERROR_CODES.BAD_USER_INPUT },
  })
}

function validateFrameId(frameId: string) {
  if (!frameId.trim()) {
    throw badInput('Frame ID must not be blank.')
  }
}

function validateVersionId(versionId: string) {
  if (
    !/^[1-9][0-9]{0,18}$/.test(versionId) ||
    BigInt(versionId) > MAX_VERSION_ID
  ) {
    throw badInput(
      'Expected version ID must be a positive 64-bit integer string.',
    )
  }
}

function toFrameData(input: FrameAttributesInput): FrameData {
  return {
    status: input.status,
    statusReason: input.statusReason ?? undefined,
    siteNo: input.siteNo ?? undefined,
    inventorySiteNo: input.inventorySiteNo ?? undefined,
    panelNumber: input.panelNumber ?? undefined,
    locationId: input.locationId ?? undefined,
    environment: input.environment ?? undefined,
    address: input.address ?? undefined,
    station: input.station ?? undefined,
    airport: input.airport ?? undefined,
    latitude: input.latitude ?? undefined,
    longitude: input.longitude ?? undefined,
    distanceToClosestSchool: input.distanceToClosestSchool ?? undefined,
    location: input.location ?? undefined,
    format: input.format ?? undefined,
    sizeCode: input.sizeCode ?? undefined,
    aspectRatioCode: input.aspectRatioCode ?? undefined,
    tSize: input.tSize ?? undefined,
    pixelHeight: input.pixelHeight ?? undefined,
    pixelWidth: input.pixelWidth ?? undefined,
    illuminationTypeId: input.illuminationTypeId ?? undefined,
    numberOfSlots: input.numberOfSlots ?? undefined,
    impactWeight: input.impactWeight ?? undefined,
    premium: input.premium ?? undefined,
    productionRateCard: input.productionRateCard ?? undefined,
    productionRateCardLegacy: input.productionRateCardLegacy ?? undefined,
    pricingGrade: input.pricingGrade ?? undefined,
  }
}

function formatTimestamp(timestamp: Timestamp__Output) {
  const date = new Date(Number(timestamp.seconds) * 1_000).toISOString()
  const fraction = String(timestamp.nanos).padStart(9, '0')
  return date.replace('.000Z', `.${fraction}Z`)
}

export function createFrameResolvers(client: FrameClient) {
  return {
    Query: {
      frames(_parent, args, { correlationId }) {
        const page = args.page ?? undefined
        const size = args.size ?? undefined

        if (page !== undefined && page < 0) {
          throw badInput('Page must be 0 or greater.')
        }

        if (size !== undefined && (size < 1 || size > 50)) {
          throw badInput('Size must be between 1 and 50.')
        }

        return callFrameRpc(
          'ListFrames',
          client.listFrames.bind(client),
          { page, size },
          correlationId,
          true,
        )
      },
      frame(_parent, { frameId }, { correlationId }) {
        validateFrameId(frameId)
        return callFrameRpc(
          'GetFrame',
          client.getFrame.bind(client),
          { frameId },
          correlationId,
          true,
        )
      },
      async frameHistory(_parent, { frameId }, { correlationId }) {
        validateFrameId(frameId)
        const history = await callFrameRpc(
          'GetFrameHistory',

import {
  Metadata,
  status,
  type CallOptions,
  type requestCallback,
  type ServiceError,
} from '@grpc/grpc-js'
import { ConstantBackoff, handleWhen, retry } from 'cockatiel'
import { GraphQLError } from 'graphql'
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto'
import { Type } from 'protobufjs'
import { GRAPHQL_ERROR_CODES } from './consts'
import type { CreateFrameRequest } from './generated/frameinventory/v1/CreateFrameRequest'
import type { DeleteFrameRequest } from './generated/frameinventory/v1/DeleteFrameRequest'
import type { Frame__Output } from './generated/frameinventory/v1/Frame'
import type { GetFrameHistoryRequest } from './generated/frameinventory/v1/GetFrameHistoryRequest'
import type { GetFrameHistoryResponse__Output } from './generated/frameinventory/v1/GetFrameHistoryResponse'
import type { GetFrameRequest } from './generated/frameinventory/v1/GetFrameRequest'
import type { ListFramesRequest } from './generated/frameinventory/v1/ListFramesRequest'
import type { ListFramesResponse__Output } from './generated/frameinventory/v1/ListFramesResponse'
import type { UpdateFrameRequest } from './generated/frameinventory/v1/UpdateFrameRequest'
import type { Empty__Output } from './generated/google/protobuf/Empty'
import { logger } from './logger'

type UnaryRpc<Request, Response> = (
  request: Request,
  metadata: Metadata,
  options: CallOptions,
  callback: requestCallback<Response>,
) => void

export interface FrameClient {
  listFrames: UnaryRpc<ListFramesRequest, ListFramesResponse__Output>
  getFrame: UnaryRpc<GetFrameRequest, Frame__Output>
  getFrameHistory: UnaryRpc<
    GetFrameHistoryRequest,
    GetFrameHistoryResponse__Output
  >
  createFrame: UnaryRpc<CreateFrameRequest, Frame__Output>
  updateFrame: UnaryRpc<UpdateFrameRequest, Frame__Output>
  deleteFrame: UnaryRpc<DeleteFrameRequest, Empty__Output>
  close(): void
}

const TIMEOUT_MS = 5_000
const readRetry = retry(
  handleWhen(
    (error) => isGrpcError(error) && error.code === status.UNAVAILABLE,
  ),
  { maxAttempts: 2, backoff: new ConstantBackoff(100) },
)

const clientErrorCodes = new Map([
  [status.INVALID_ARGUMENT, GRAPHQL_ERROR_CODES.BAD_USER_INPUT],
  [status.NOT_FOUND, GRAPHQL_ERROR_CODES.NOT_FOUND],
  [status.ALREADY_EXISTS, GRAPHQL_ERROR_CODES.ALREADY_EXISTS],
  [status.ABORTED, GRAPHQL_ERROR_CODES.CONFLICT],
])

const statusDetailsType = Type.fromJSON('Status', {
  fields: {
    details: { rule: 'repeated', type: 'Any', id: 3 },
  },
  nested: {
    Any: {
      fields: {
        typeUrl: { type: 'string', id: 1 },
        value: { type: 'bytes', id: 2 },
      },
    },
  },
})
const badRequestType = Type.fromJSON('BadRequest', {
  fields: {
    fieldViolations: { rule: 'repeated', type: 'FieldViolation', id: 1 },
  },
  nested: {
    FieldViolation: {
      fields: {
        field: { type: 'string', id: 1 },
        description: { type: 'string', id: 2 },
      },
    },
  },
})

function fieldViolations(
  error: unknown,
): { field: string; description: string }[] {
  if (
    !(error instanceof Error) ||
    !('metadata' in error) ||
    !(error.metadata instanceof Metadata)
  ) {
    return []
  }
  const trailer = error.metadata.get('grpc-status-details-bin')[0]
  if (!Buffer.isBuffer(trailer)) return []

  try {
    const decoded = statusDetailsType.decode(trailer) as unknown as {
      details?: { typeUrl?: string; value?: Uint8Array }[]
    }
    return (decoded.details ?? []).flatMap((detail) => {
      if (
        !detail.typeUrl?.endsWith('/google.rpc.BadRequest') ||
        !detail.value
      ) {
        return []
      }
      try {
        const badRequest = badRequestType.decode(detail.value) as unknown as {
          fieldViolations?: { field?: string; description?: string }[]
        }
        return (badRequest.fieldViolations ?? []).map((violation) => ({
          field: violation.field ?? '',
          description: violation.description ?? '',
        }))
      } catch {
        return []
      }
    })
  } catch {
    return []
  }
}

function isGrpcError(
  error: unknown,
): error is Pick<ServiceError, 'code' | 'details'> {
  return (
    error instanceof Error &&
    'code' in error &&
    typeof error.code === 'number' &&
    'details' in error &&
    typeof error.details === 'string'
  )
}

export async function callFrameRpc<Request, Response>(
  method: string,
  rpc: UnaryRpc<Request, Response>,
  request: Request,
  correlationId: string = randomUUID(),
  retryUnavailable = false,
): Promise<Response> {
  const metadata = new Metadata()
  metadata.set('x-correlation-id', correlationId)
  const rpcLogger = logger.child({ correlationId })
  const startedAt = performance.now()
  const deadline = Date.now() + TIMEOUT_MS
  const call = () =>
    new Promise<Response>((resolve, reject) => {
      rpc(request, metadata, { deadline }, (error, response) => {
        if (error) {
          reject(error)
        } else if (!response) {
          reject(new Error('gRPC returned no response'))
        } else {
          resolve(response)
        }
      })
    })

  try {
    const response = retryUnavailable
      ? await readRetry.execute(call, AbortSignal.timeout(TIMEOUT_MS))
      : await call()
    rpcLogger.debug(
      { method, durationMs: performance.now() - startedAt },
      'Frame RPC completed',
    )
    return response
  } catch (error) {
    const durationMs = performance.now() - startedAt
    const grpcError = isGrpcError(error) ? error : undefined

    if (grpcError) {
      const code = clientErrorCodes.get(grpcError.code)
      if (code) {
        rpcLogger.debug(
          { method, grpcCode: grpcError.code, durationMs },
          'Frame RPC rejected',
        )
        const violations =
          grpcError.code === status.INVALID_ARGUMENT
            ? fieldViolations(error)
            : []
        throw new GraphQLError(grpcError.details, {
          extensions: {
            code,
            ...(violations.length > 0 ? { fieldViolations: violations } : {}),
          },
        })
      }

      if (
        grpcError.code === status.UNAVAILABLE ||
        grpcError.code === status.DEADLINE_EXCEEDED
      ) {
        rpcLogger.warn(
          { method, grpcCode: grpcError.code, durationMs },
          'Frame service is unavailable',
        )
        throw new GraphQLError('Frame service is unavailable', {
          extensions: { code: GRAPHQL_ERROR_CODES.SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE },
        })
      }
    }

    rpcLogger.error(
      { method, grpcCode: grpcError?.code, durationMs },
      'Frame RPC failed',
    )
    throw new GraphQLError('Frame operation failed', {
      extensions: { code: GRAPHQL_ERROR_CODES.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR },
    })
  }
}
