# Bulk CSV inventory import

Author: Alex Callow
Date: 2026-11-26

## Overview

An inventory operator uploads inventory_frame.csv directly to S3 using a presigned URL. The BFF delegates job creation to Spring Boot, which records AWAITING_UPLOAD and assigns uploads/{jobId}/inventory_frame.csv. An S3-triggered Lambda sends the upload event to SQS. Spring Boot moves the job to PENDING and starts Temporal workflow csv-import-{jobId}. SQS retries failed delivery and a DLQ listener records dispatch failures.

The worker streams the CSV into job-scoped UNLOGGED PostgreSQL staging in batches and heartbeats during loading. It records invalid rows in import_row_errors and applies set-based writes with MERGE RETURNING where appropriate. The proposed six-table target and frame history must be reconciled with the repository's existing versioned schema. Inventory changes and outbox records must commit together.

## Agreed import behavior

- A newer source timestamp creates a version. An equal timestamp and matching content hash is a no-op. An older timestamp produces STALE_RECORD. An equal timestamp with different content produces TIMESTAMP_COLLISION_CONFLICT and records both hashes. Skipped conflicts result in COMPLETED_WITH_ERRORS.
- The explicit forceOverwrite flag accepts stale and same-timestamp conflicts. The new version preserves source_modified_date and records FORCED_OVERWRITE and import_job_id. Close and open at one database-generated boundary strictly later than the locked current valid_from.
- DELTA is the default and leaves absent frames alone. FULL_SNAPSHOT requires an explicit GLOBAL scope or validated partition scope using country, region or environment. Every identifiable frame ID in the file counts as present, including rows with invalid payloads.
- FULL_SNAPSHOT soft-retires absent active frames in scope with MISSING_FROM_FULL_SNAPSHOT. Abort if more than 10% of scoped active frames would retire. A malformed-row rate above 5% must prevent retirement. Whether to fail the whole snapshot is open.

## Analysis

All seven Goldfish lenses completed review. The recommendations below are proposed decisions for RFC alignment.

### Delivery and recovery

- Bind each job to one immutable object. Sign the exact key and the create-only PUT condition (If-None-Match: *), enable S3 versioning, and persist the accepted version ID so every retry reads the same bytes. Keep the object through the retry and reconciliation window. Validate the bucket, decoded key, object version, and size before dispatch. [S3 conditional writes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/conditional-writes.html) [S3 event delivery](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/notification-how-to-event-types-and-destinations.html)
- Record PENDING conditionally, invoke Temporal with the job-derived workflow ID, and acknowledge SQS only after start or after confirming the same job's workflow already exists. Configure both running-ID conflict and closed-ID reuse policies. A crash between the DB write and Temporal start leaves a retryable PENDING job. A lost start response must be reconciled before any DLQ transition to FAILED. Guard terminal states and fence a late starter with conditional job transitions before it can apply inventory. Reconcile old AWAITING_UPLOAD and PENDING jobs against S3 and Temporal, and cover Lambda delivery failures separately from consumer DLQ failures. [Temporal workflow ID policies](https://docs.temporal.io/develop/java/nexus/development-walkthrough/send-messages)
- Stage by job ID, attempt generation, and logical CSV row number. Record observed frame IDs independently of row validity. Mark a generation complete only after EOF and verify that its completion marker and counts still match before applying. Keep the marker in unlogged storage with the staged rows so recovery clears both, and reload from the bound S3 version when the marker is missing. Use heartbeats for liveness and cancellation. Restart the stream for an incomplete generation in the first release. Record row errors durably with stable keys so retries do not duplicate errors. [PostgreSQL unlogged tables](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-createtable.html)

### Inventory apply

- Reuse the existing stable-frame lock, current-version uniqueness constraint, and close-and-append history. The repository already computes a boundary as the greater of database wall-clock time and the current valid_from plus one microsecond, then uses that boundary for the next version. Reuse this rule for all imported changes, including retirements. Preserve source_modified_at separately. The existing schema already stores versioned external references and links. Map each of the 45 CSV fields before adding new tables or moving attributes. Keep immutable history when normalizing shared site or spec data. [Schema](../frame-inventory-schema/frame-inventory-schema.md) [Repository](../../src/backend/src/main/java/com/global/ct/frameinventory/frame/FrameRepository.java)
- Define the content hash over canonical typed values, including versioned links and external references. Specify normalization, timezone and precision, null behavior, and duplicate-ID handling. Change manual UI/API writes to set source_modified_at from statement_timestamp() on the version insert after obtaining the frame lock. Preserve the source timestamp on CSV imports, including forced overwrites. Define how comparisons handle legacy manual versions that inherited an older source timestamp. A forced overwrite can move the current source timestamp backward. A separate source high-water mark remains an open decision.
- Build one candidate per target key before set-based writes. Resolve shared dimensions and reserve frame identities before opening dependent versions and links. PostgreSQL 18 supports MERGE RETURNING, but a source candidate takes only one action, so close and append in separate set-based statements in the same transaction. Use the actual changed version IDs to produce outbox records. Commit versions, links, outbox, and final job status together. A retry after a lost commit response returns the committed result. [PostgreSQL MERGE](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-merge.html)
- Compute the retirement numerator and denominator on the same protected pre-apply inventory view. Row locks protect existing IDs, while new frames and edits that move into or out of scope require a shared writer protocol. Start with a transaction-scoped inventory lock held in shared mode by manual writes and DELTA applies, and in exclusive mode by snapshots. Take per-frame locks in stable ID order. This serializes promotion of snapshots even when their scopes are disjoint. Keep it out of upload, parsing, and staging. Measure lock time before enabling the feature. Never infer absence from a partial stream or an unrecoverable CSV parse error. Decide whether unidentifiable rows, scope violations, and header-only snapshots fail the whole job. The proposed default is to fail a snapshot before any inventory write when a safety check fails.

### Snapshot watermark

- Persist snapshot_as_of on the job. Accept a producer-supplied export watermark at job creation. When omitted, derive it from MAX(modified_date) after scanning the complete file. Use one documented source timezone and precision for comparisons. Require the exporter to supply an explicit watermark when the file cannot establish one. MAX(modified_date) measures the newest row change and can lag the time a complete export was generated. It also cannot prove completeness, so prefer the explicit export watermark for feeds where these times differ.
- Use canonical scope keys in a containment hierarchy: GLOBAL, country, country/region, and country/region/environment. Require a region for every environment-level FULL_SNAPSHOT in the first release. Reject a country/environment scope such as UK/UNDERGROUND at job creation. An operator can export a separate authoritative snapshot for each region or use DELTA for a cross-region file.
- Before inventory writes and under the snapshot apply lock, reject a watermark outside the freshness window (proposed default 24 hours), in the future beyond allowed clock skew, or strictly below the maximum committed watermark for the requested scope and its ancestors. Equal watermarks pass this check. On successful commit, advance only the requested scope's watermark, including when the job completes with row errors. A failed job leaves all watermarks as they were.
- A newer descendant watermark does not reject an enclosing snapshot. Apply normal row conflict checks throughout the requested scope, including newer child scopes. Before retiring absent frames, exclude the entire subtree of each descendant whose committed watermark is strictly newer than the incoming watermark. Report the protected scopes and skipped retirement count. A descendant at the same watermark remains eligible. For example, a GLOBAL export at 11:30 can apply after a partition snapshot at 12:00, with retirement excluded in that partition. A partition export at 11:00 fails if an ancestor already committed at 12:00.
- Among the remaining absent active frames, exclude any whose current valid_from or source_modified_at is after snapshot_as_of and record SKIPPED_RETIREMENT_NEWER_THAN_SNAPSHOT. This protects newer current versions, including edits within the same scope. Count only eligible retirements in the 10% numerator and keep the denominator as all pre-apply active frames in the declared scope. Capture the watermark checks, both exclusion counts, the breaker calculation, and the scope watermark update in the same protected apply transaction.

### Snapshot history and reactivation

The agreed representation is a new current version with status RETIRED and reason MISSING_FROM_FULL_SNAPSHOT. Define how current inventory queries treat that version and how a later import reactivates it. Existing manual deletion closes the last current version without opening a replacement. Keep those behaviors explicit in the status and history contract. If snapshot closure sets closed_by_change_source, extend the V2 constraint, which currently allows only MANUAL_DELETE. [V2 migration](../../src/backend/src/main/resources/db/migration/V2__add_frame_change_source.sql)

## Goals and non-goals

- Deliver authenticated upload, visible job progress and row errors, retry-safe imports, audited versions, scoped retirement, and transactional outbox records.
- Leave mass deletion, generalized CSV mapping, automatic repair of malformed source values, and multi-scope FULL_SNAPSHOT uploads outside the first release. If authoritative cross-region exports become a regular need, consider one atomic job over explicitly named scopes, each with its own watermark and retirement check.

## Alternatives weighed

- Keep the S3-to-Lambda bridge as requested. Direct S3-to-SQS delivery could remove an operational failure path if the bridge only forwards events. Verify what routing or event normalization the Lambda needs to own.
- Keep UNLOGGED staging with full source replay for initial implementation. Durable staging could reduce replay cost and operational complexity after failover, at the cost of logging intermediate data. Benchmark with the expected maximum file.
- Reuse versioned history as the initial design direction. Add a separate frame_history table only if it serves a distinct audited need. Otherwise two history stores would require agreement on which is authoritative.

## Key decisions and implementation sequence

1. Map the CSV to the current schema and the proposed six entities. Resolve source timestamp parsing, manual-edit ordering, force authorization, link semantics, duplicate IDs, and schema ownership before migrations.
2. Add durable job, row error, lineage, and outbox storage through additive Flyway migrations. Expose BFF job creation and status, including counts, fatal errors, and paginated row errors. Set upload-size, row-count, timeout, and retention limits from the agreed operating envelope.
3. Implement the S3 event bridge, SQS dispatch and DLQ, and Temporal start. Exercise duplicate notifications, late events, ambiguous starts, and reconciliation before applying inventory.
4. Implement staging and atomic DELTA apply. Run the supplied CSV against PostgreSQL 18 and check replay, timestamp collisions, manual edits, forced overwrite, malformed quoting, duplicate IDs, lost staging, and worker failure immediately after commit.
5. Add scoped FULL_SNAPSHOT with a protected retirement calculation. Verify that malformed rows with IDs stay present, out-of-scope frames stay untouched, and the exact 5% and 10% boundaries behave as agreed. Exercise rejection of environment scopes without a region, expired and out-of-order watermarks, watermark equality, derived watermarks, newer ancestors rejecting narrower snapshots, newer descendants protecting entire subtrees while present rows still upsert, frames created or moved into scope after export, and concurrent manual writes. Roll out DELTA first, then enable snapshot after observing apply times and reviewing operator safeguards.
6. Track queue age and DLQ depth, time in each job state, staging retries, apply transaction duration, row error codes, retirement guard trips, and outbox lag. Correlate logs by job ID and keep presigned URLs and raw row content out of logs.

# Frame Inventory — Exercise Instructions

## 1. Scenario

In the **out-of-home (OOH) media** industry, advertisers buy time on physical
display surfaces such as roadside billboards, transport platforms, mall
screens, and bus shelters. Each surface is referred to as a **frame**, and an
operator's catalogue of frames — including their location, size, format,
status, and commercial attributes — is collectively known as the **frame
inventory**. Keeping that inventory accurate matters: every downstream process
(planning, pricing, booking, reporting) depends on it.

For this exercise the candidate will build a small but realistic service for
managing OOH frame inventory. Scoping is part of the exercise: the candidate
is not expected to deliver every feature one could imagine, but to pick a
meaningful subset and deliver it well.

## 2. What we provide

This repository is the starting point. It is intentionally minimal so the
candidate can make their own architectural choices, but it includes enough
infrastructure to skip the boilerplate and start delivering business value
straight away.

| Path                  | Contents                                                                          |
| --------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `src/backend/`        | Bare Spring Boot 3.5 + Java 21 module (Gradle). Exposes only `/api/health`.       |
| `src/frontend/`       | Next.js + React 19 + TypeScript module that calls the backend `/api/health` on boot. |
| `docker-compose.yml`  | One-command infra: backend, frontend, MongoDB, Postgres, OpenSearch + Dashboards.  |
| `data/`               | Extract from the legacy system — `inventory_frame.csv` (~1.3k OOH frame rows).    |
| `design-system/`      | Design system the frontend must be built against — components, tokens, guidance.  |
| `README.md`           | How to run the stack locally, ports, and credentials for the bundled services.    |

> **A note on the suggested infrastructure.** The `docker-compose.yml` file
> is a starting point, not a requirement. The candidate is free to swap any
> of these services for tooling they prefer (a different database, search
> engine, message broker, hosting model, etc.) as long as the final stack
> still runs end-to-end with a single command. If the candidate does choose
> to use the services provided here, they should pick **one** of the two
> datastores for their domain data — either `mongodb` *or* `postgres`,
> not both — and remove the service they don't need (along with its volume)
> so the stack reflects the design actually built.

In addition, the candidate receives:

- A **provisioned OpenAI Codex API key**. Use of an AI coding assistant is
  explicitly expected — we want to see how the candidate collaborates with a
  model, not whether they can hand-write every line.

## 3. Features

The candidate should deliver the following features:

1. **Add a frame.** A user can create a new frame through the application and
   see it persisted in the inventory.
2. **Edit a frame.** A user can amend an existing frame's attributes and have
   the changes saved.
3. **Bulk upload frames from a CSV.** A user can upload a CSV through the
   application and have the rows ingested into the inventory. The supplied
   `data/inventory_frame.csv` is the file to validate this feature
   against. This is a user-driven feature of the running app, not a one-off
   bootstrap step.
4. **View a frame's history.** A user can see the audit trail of changes to
   any given frame.

How these features are surfaced, structured, and tested is left to the
candidate's judgement.

## 4. Domain data

The shape of a frame is anchored by the legacy export shipped at
`data/inventory_frame.csv` (~1,300 rows) and by the prototype in
`design-system/`. The candidate is expected to inspect both and design a
domain model they are comfortable defending.

At a high level, each frame in the export carries:

- **Identity** — a frame identifier, plus references to downstream systems
  (Broadsign, pricing, linked frames).
- **Location** — country, region, town, postcode, latitude/longitude,
  address, and distance to the nearest school.
- **Site & position** — the kind of place the frame lives in (station,
  underground, roadside, airport, etc.) and where on that site it sits.
- **Format** — classic vs digital, format code, dimensions / pixels /
  aspect ratio, illumination, number of slots, size grouping.
- **Lifecycle** — created/modified timestamps, status, and a status reason.
- **Commercials** — impact weight, pricing grade, production rate card,
  premium flag.

The legacy column names and groupings are not prescriptive — the candidate
should design the domain model that best fits the features in §3, and
document the assumptions they made along the way.

## 5. Additional Requirements

Install and use the **[Entire CLI](https://entire.io)**. Entire hooks into the
candidate's git workflow and, on every push, captures the Codex agent
sessions that produced the changes and links them to the corresponding
commits as *checkpoints*. The result is a searchable record of how the
solution was actually built: the prompts used, the iterations the candidate
went through, the suggestions they accepted, and — just as important — the
ones they rejected or refined.

This is not about surveillance; it is about giving us a fair signal of
**how** the candidate works with AI tooling. We are far less interested in
whether code came from a human keystroke or a model completion than in
whether the candidate exercised judgement, scoped well, and reviewed the
output critically.

> **Note:** Codex support in Entire is currently in preview. The candidate
> should follow Entire's setup documentation for the latest supported
> workflow.

## 6. Submission

When the candidate is ready, they should share a **public GitHub repository**
containing their solution. The repository must include:

- All source code and anything else required to run the solution.
- A README explaining how to run it, the design decisions taken, and the
  trade-offs made.
- The Entire **checkpoints branch** with the captured Codex sessions linked
  to commits, so we can review the AI collaboration alongside the code.

There is no fixed deadline; we recommend timeboxing the exercise to a few
focused sessions rather than open-ended work. If something blocks progress,
note it in the README rather than over-investing time on it.

Introduction
Section titled “Introduction”
When you’re developing cloud and serverless applications, you need to grant access to various AWS resources like S3 buckets and RDS databases.
To handle this, you create IAM roles and assign permissions through policies.
However, configuring these policies can be challenging, especially if you want to ensure minimal access of all principals to your resources.
LocalStack IAM Policy Stream automates the generation of IAM policies for your AWS API requests on your local machine.
This stream helps you identify the necessary permissions for your cloud application and allows you to detect logical errors, such as unexpected actions in your policies.
This tutorial will guide you through setting up IAM Policy Stream for a locally running AWS application.
We’ll use a basic example involving an S3 bucket, an SQS queue, and a bucket notification configuration.
You’ll generate the policy for the bucket notification configuration and insert it into the SQS queue.
Why use IAM Policy Stream?
Section titled “Why use IAM Policy Stream?”
LocalStack enables you to create and enforce local IAM roles and policies using the ENFORCE_IAM feature.
However, users often struggle to figure out the necessary permissions for different actions.
It’s important to find a balance, avoiding giving too many permissions while making sure the right ones are granted.
This challenge becomes more complex when dealing with AWS services that make requests not directly visible to users.
For instance, if an SNS topic sends a message to an SQS queue and the underlying call fails, there might be no clear error message, causing confusion, especially for those less familiar with the services.
IAM Policy Stream simplifies this by automatically generating the needed policies and showing them to users.
This makes it easier to integrate with resources, roles, and users, streamlining the development process.
Additionally, it serves as a useful learning tool, helping users understand the permissions linked to various AWS calls and improving the onboarding experience for newcomers to AWS.

The following diagram illustrates the architecture of this tutorial:
In this architecture:

Tutorial: Configure an S3 bucket for event notifications using SQS
Section titled “Tutorial: Configure an S3 bucket for event notifications using SQS”
In this tutorial, you will configure a LocalStack S3 bucket to send event notifications to an SQS queue.
You will then use IAM Policy Stream to generate the necessary IAM policy for the SQS queue.
You will use Terraform to create the resources and the AWS CLI to interact with them.
With LocalStack’s IAM enforcement enabled, you can thoroughly test your policy and ensure that the development setup mirrors the production environment.
Start your LocalStack container
Section titled “Start your LocalStack container”
Launch the LocalStack container on your local machine using the specified command:
Terminal window
LOCALSTACK_DEBUG=1 LOCALSTACK_IAM_SOFT_MODE=1 lstk start
In the above command:
LOCALSTACK_DEBUG=1 turns on detailed logging to check API calls and IAM violations.
LOCALSTACK_IAM_SOFT_MODE=1 lets you test IAM enforcement by logging violations without stopping the API calls.
Create the Terraform configuration
Section titled “Create the Terraform configuration”
Create a new file called main.tf for the Terraform setup of an S3 bucket and an SQS queue.
Start by using the aws_sqs_queue resource to create an SQS queue named s3-event-notification-queue.
resource "aws_sqs_queue" "queue" {
name = "s3-event-notification-queue"
}
Next, use the aws_s3_bucket resource to create an S3 bucket called s3-event-notification-bucket.
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "bucket" {
bucket = "s3-event-notification-bucket"
}
Finally, use the aws_s3_bucket_notification resource to link the S3 bucket with the SQS queue for sending notifications:
resource "aws_s3_bucket_notification" "bucket_notification" {
bucket = aws_s3_bucket.bucket.id
queue {
queue_arn = aws_sqs_queue.queue.arn
events = ["s3:ObjectCreated:*"]
}
}
Deploy the Terraform configuration
Section titled “Deploy the Terraform configuration”
You can use lstk terraform to deploy your Terraform configuration within the LocalStack environment.
Run the following commands to initialize and apply the Terraform configuration:
Terminal window
lstk terraform init
lstk terraform apply
You will be prompted to confirm the changes.

import type { UpdateFrameRequest } from './generated/frameinventory/v1/UpdateFrameRequest'
import type { Empty__Output } from './generated/google/protobuf/Empty'
import { logger } from './logger'

type UnaryRpc<Request, Response> = (
  request: Request,
  metadata: Metadata,
  options: CallOptions,
  callback: requestCallback<Response>,
) => void

export interface FrameClient {
  listFrames: UnaryRpc<ListFramesRequest, ListFramesResponse__Output>

const TIMEOUT_MS = 5_000
const readRetry = retry(
  handleWhen(
    (error) => isGrpcError(error) && error.code === status.UNAVAILABLE,
  ),
  { maxAttempts: 2, backoff: new ConstantBackoff(100) },
)

const clientErrorCodes = new Map([
  [status.INVALID_ARGUMENT, GRAPHQL_ERROR_CODES.BAD_USER_INPUT],
  [status.NOT_FOUND, GRAPHQL_ERROR_CODES.NOT_FOUND],
  [status.ALREADY_EXISTS, GRAPHQL_ERROR_CODES.ALREADY_EXISTS],
  [status.ABORTED, GRAPHQL_ERROR_CODES.CONFLICT],
])

const statusDetailsType = Type.fromJSON('Status', {
  fields: {
    details: { rule: 'repeated', type: 'Any', id: 3 },
  },
  nested: {
    Any: {
      fields: {
        typeUrl: { type: 'string', id: 1 },
        value: { type: 'bytes', id: 2 },
      },
    },
  },
})
const badRequestType = Type.fromJSON('BadRequest', {
  fields: {
    fieldViolations: { rule: 'repeated', type: 'FieldViolation', id: 1 },
  },
  nested: {
    FieldViolation: {
      fields: {
        field: { type: 'string', id: 1 },
        description: { type: 'string', id: 2 },
      },
    },
  },
})

function fieldViolations(
  error: unknown,
): { field: string; description: string }[] {
  if (
    !(error instanceof Error) ||
    !('metadata' in error) ||
    !(error.metadata instanceof Metadata)
  ) {
    return []
  }
  const trailer = error.metadata.get('grpc-status-details-bin')[0]
  if (!Buffer.isBuffer(trailer)) return []

  try {
    const decoded = statusDetailsType.decode(trailer) as unknown as {
      details?: { typeUrl?: string; value?: Uint8Array }[]
    }
    return (decoded.details ?? []).flatMap((detail) => {
      if (
        !detail.typeUrl?.endsWith('/google.rpc.BadRequest') ||
        !detail.value
      ) {
        return []
      }
      try {
        const badRequest = badRequestType.decode(detail.value) as unknown as {
          fieldViolations?: { field?: string; description?: string }[]
        }
        return (badRequest.fieldViolations ?? []).map((violation) => ({
          field: violation.field ?? '',
          description: violation.description ?? '',
        }))
      } catch {
        return []
      }
    })
  } catch {
    return []
  }
}

function isGrpcError(
  error: unknown,
): error is Pick<ServiceError, 'code' | 'details'> {
  return (
    error instanceof Error &&
    'code' in error &&
    typeof error.code === 'number' &&
    'details' in error &&
    typeof error.details === 'string'
  )
}

export async function callFrameRpc<Request, Response>(
  method: string,
  rpc: UnaryRpc<Request, Response>,
  request: Request,
  correlationId: string = randomUUID(),
  retryUnavailable = false,
): Promise<Response> {
  const metadata = new Metadata()
  metadata.set('x-correlation-id', correlationId)
  const rpcLogger = logger.child({ correlationId })
  const startedAt = performance.now()
  const deadline = Date.now() + TIMEOUT_MS
  const call = () =>
    new Promise<Response>((resolve, reject) => {
      rpc(request, metadata, { deadline }, (error, response) => {
        if (error) {
          reject(error)
        } else if (!response) {
          reject(new Error('gRPC returned no response'))
        } else {
          resolve(response)
        }
      })
    })

  try {
    const response = retryUnavailable
      ? await readRetry.execute(call, AbortSignal.timeout(TIMEOUT_MS))
      : await call()
    rpcLogger.debug(
      { method, durationMs: performance.now() - startedAt },
      'Frame RPC completed',
    )
    return response
  } catch (error) {
    const durationMs = performance.now() - startedAt
    const grpcError = isGrpcError(error) ? error : undefined

    if (grpcError) {
      const code = clientErrorCodes.get(grpcError.code)
      if (code) {
        rpcLogger.debug(
          { method, grpcCode: grpcError.code, durationMs },
          'Frame RPC rejected',
        )
        const violations =
          grpcError.code === status.INVALID_ARGUMENT
            ? fieldViolations(error)
            : []
        throw new GraphQLError(grpcError.details, {
          extensions: {
            code,
            ...(violations.length > 0 ? { fieldViolations: violations } : {}),
          },
        })
      }

      if (
        grpcError.code === status.UNAVAILABLE ||
        grpcError.code === status.DEADLINE_EXCEEDED
      ) {
        rpcLogger.warn(
          { method, grpcCode: grpcError.code, durationMs },
          'Frame service is unavailable',
        )
        throw new GraphQLError('Frame service is unavailable', {
          extensions: { code: GRAPHQL_ERROR_CODES.SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE },
        })
      }
    }

    rpcLogger.error(
      { method, grpcCode: grpcError?.code, durationMs },
      'Frame RPC failed',
    )
    throw new GraphQLError('Frame operation failed', {
      extensions: { code: GRAPHQL_ERROR_CODES.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR },
    })
  }
}

# Bulk CSV inventory import

Author: Alex Callow
Date: 2026-11-26

## Overview

An inventory operator uploads inventory_frame.csv directly to S3 using a presigned URL. The BFF delegates job creation to Spring Boot, which records AWAITING_UPLOAD and assigns uploads/{jobId}/inventory_frame.csv. An S3-triggered Lambda sends the upload event to SQS. Spring Boot moves the job to PENDING and starts Temporal workflow csv-import-{jobId}. SQS retries failed delivery and a DLQ listener records dispatch failures.

The worker streams the CSV into job-scoped UNLOGGED PostgreSQL staging in batches and heartbeats during loading. It records invalid rows in import_row_errors and applies set-based writes with MERGE RETURNING where appropriate. The proposed six-table target and frame history must be reconciled with the repository's existing versioned schema. Inventory changes and outbox records must commit together.

## Agreed import behavior

- A newer source timestamp creates a version. An equal timestamp and matching content hash is a no-op. An older timestamp produces STALE_RECORD. An equal timestamp with different content produces TIMESTAMP_COLLISION_CONFLICT and records both hashes. Skipped conflicts result in COMPLETED_WITH_ERRORS.
- The explicit forceOverwrite flag accepts stale and same-timestamp conflicts. The new version preserves source_modified_date and records FORCED_OVERWRITE and import_job_id. Close and open at one database-generated boundary strictly later than the locked current valid_from.
- DELTA is the default and leaves absent frames alone. FULL_SNAPSHOT requires an explicit GLOBAL scope or validated partition scope using country, region or environment. Every identifiable frame ID in the file counts as present, including rows with invalid payloads.
- FULL_SNAPSHOT soft-retires absent active frames in scope with MISSING_FROM_FULL_SNAPSHOT. Abort if more than 10% of scoped active frames would retire. A malformed-row rate above 5% must prevent retirement. Whether to fail the whole snapshot is open.

## Analysis

All seven Goldfish lenses completed review. The recommendations below are proposed decisions for RFC alignment.

### Delivery and recovery

- Bind each job to one immutable object. Sign the exact key and the create-only PUT condition (If-None-Match: *), enable S3 versioning, and persist the accepted version ID so every retry reads the same bytes. Keep the object through the retry and reconciliation window. Validate the bucket, decoded key, object version, and size before dispatch. [S3 conditional writes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/conditional-writes.html) [S3 event delivery](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/notification-how-to-event-types-and-destinations.html)
- Record PENDING conditionally, invoke Temporal with the job-derived workflow ID, and acknowledge SQS only after start or after confirming the same job's workflow already exists. Configure both running-ID conflict and closed-ID reuse policies. A crash between the DB write and Temporal start leaves a retryable PENDING job. A lost start response must be reconciled before any DLQ transition to FAILED. Guard terminal states and fence a late starter with conditional job transitions before it can apply inventory. Reconcile old AWAITING_UPLOAD and PENDING jobs against S3 and Temporal, and cover Lambda delivery failures separately from consumer DLQ failures. [Temporal workflow ID policies](https://docs.temporal.io/develop/java/nexus/development-walkthrough/send-messages)
- Stage by job ID, attempt generation, and logical CSV row number. Record observed frame IDs independently of row validity. Mark a generation complete only after EOF and verify that its completion marker and counts still match before applying. Keep the marker in unlogged storage with the staged rows so recovery clears both, and reload from the bound S3 version when the marker is missing. Use heartbeats for liveness and cancellation. Restart the stream for an incomplete generation in the first release. Record row errors durably with stable keys so retries do not duplicate errors. [PostgreSQL unlogged tables](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-createtable.html)

### Inventory apply

- Reuse the existing stable-frame lock, current-version uniqueness constraint, and close-and-append history. The repository already computes a boundary as the greater of database wall-clock time and the current valid_from plus one microsecond, then uses that boundary for the next version. Reuse this rule for all imported changes, including retirements. Preserve source_modified_at separately. The existing schema already stores versioned external references and links. Map each of the 45 CSV fields before adding new tables or moving attributes. Keep immutable history when normalizing shared site or spec data. [Schema](../frame-inventory-schema/frame-inventory-schema.md) [Repository](../../src/backend/src/main/java/com/global/ct/frameinventory/frame/FrameRepository.java)
- Define the content hash over canonical typed values, including versioned links and external references. Specify normalization, timezone and precision, null behavior, and duplicate-ID handling. Change manual UI/API writes to set source_modified_at from statement_timestamp() on the version insert after obtaining the frame lock. Preserve the source timestamp on CSV imports, including forced overwrites. Define how comparisons handle legacy manual versions that inherited an older source timestamp. A forced overwrite can move the current source timestamp backward. A separate source high-water mark remains an open decision.
- Build one candidate per target key before set-based writes. Resolve shared dimensions and reserve frame identities before opening dependent versions and links. PostgreSQL 18 supports MERGE RETURNING, but a source candidate takes only one action, so close and append in separate set-based statements in the same transaction. Use the actual changed version IDs to produce outbox records. Commit versions, links, outbox, and final job status together. A retry after a lost commit response returns the committed result. [PostgreSQL MERGE](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-merge.html)
- Compute the retirement numerator and denominator on the same protected pre-apply inventory view. Row locks protect existing IDs, while new frames and edits that move into or out of scope require a shared writer protocol. Start with a transaction-scoped inventory lock held in shared mode by manual writes and DELTA applies, and in exclusive mode by snapshots. Take per-frame locks in stable ID order. This serializes promotion of snapshots even when their scopes are disjoint. Keep it out of upload, parsing, and staging. Measure lock time before enabling the feature. Never infer absence from a partial stream or an unrecoverable CSV parse error. Decide whether unidentifiable rows, scope violations, and header-only snapshots fail the whole job. The proposed default is to fail a snapshot before any inventory write when a safety check fails.

### Snapshot watermark

- Persist snapshot_as_of on the job. Accept a producer-supplied export watermark at job creation. When omitted, derive it from MAX(modified_date) after scanning the complete file. Use one documented source timezone and precision for comparisons. Require the exporter to supply an explicit watermark when the file cannot establish one. MAX(modified_date) measures the newest row change and can lag the time a complete export was generated. It also cannot prove completeness, so prefer the explicit export watermark for feeds where these times differ.
- Use canonical scope keys in a containment hierarchy: GLOBAL, country, country/region, and country/region/environment. Require a region for every environment-level FULL_SNAPSHOT in the first release. Reject a country/environment scope such as UK/UNDERGROUND at job creation. An operator can export a separate authoritative snapshot for each region or use DELTA for a cross-region file.
- Before inventory writes and under the snapshot apply lock, reject a watermark outside the freshness window (proposed default 24 hours), in the future beyond allowed clock skew, or strictly below the maximum committed watermark for the requested scope and its ancestors. Equal watermarks pass this check. On successful commit, advance only the requested scope's watermark, including when the job completes with row errors. A failed job leaves all watermarks as they were.
- A newer descendant watermark does not reject an enclosing snapshot. Apply normal row conflict checks throughout the requested scope, including newer child scopes. Before retiring absent frames, exclude the entire subtree of each descendant whose committed watermark is strictly newer than the incoming watermark. Report the protected scopes and skipped retirement count. A descendant at the same watermark remains eligible. For example, a GLOBAL export at 11:30 can apply after a partition snapshot at 12:00, with retirement excluded in that partition. A partition export at 11:00 fails if an ancestor already committed at 12:00.
- Among the remaining absent active frames, exclude any whose current valid_from or source_modified_at is after snapshot_as_of and record SKIPPED_RETIREMENT_NEWER_THAN_SNAPSHOT. This protects newer current versions, including edits within the same scope. Count only eligible retirements in the 10% numerator and keep the denominator as all pre-apply active frames in the declared scope. Capture the watermark checks, both exclusion counts, the breaker calculation, and the scope watermark update in the same protected apply transaction.

### Snapshot history and reactivation

The agreed representation is a new current version with status RETIRED and reason MISSING_FROM_FULL_SNAPSHOT. Define how current inventory queries treat that version and how a later import reactivates it. Existing manual deletion closes the last current version without opening a replacement. Keep those behaviors explicit in the status and history contract. If snapshot closure sets closed_by_change_source, extend the V2 constraint, which currently allows only MANUAL_DELETE. [V2 migration](../../src/backend/src/main/resources/db/migration/V2__add_frame_change_source.sql)

## Goals and non-goals

- Deliver authenticated upload, visible job progress and row errors, retry-safe imports, audited versions, scoped retirement, and transactional outbox records.
- Leave mass deletion, generalized CSV mapping, automatic repair of malformed source values, and multi-scope FULL_SNAPSHOT uploads outside the first release. If authoritative cross-region exports become a regular need, consider one atomic job over explicitly named scopes, each with its own watermark and retirement check.

## Alternatives weighed

- Keep the S3-to-Lambda bridge as requested. Direct S3-to-SQS delivery could remove an operational failure path if the bridge only forwards events. Verify what routing or event normalization the Lambda needs to own.
- Keep UNLOGGED staging with full source replay for initial implementation. Durable staging could reduce replay cost and operational complexity after failover, at the cost of logging intermediate data. Benchmark with the expected maximum file.
- Reuse versioned history as the initial design direction. Add a separate frame_history table only if it serves a distinct audited need. Otherwise two history stores would require agreement on which is authoritative.

## Key decisions and implementation sequence

1. Map the CSV to the current schema and the proposed six entities. Resolve source timestamp parsing, manual-edit ordering, force authorization, link semantics, duplicate IDs, and schema ownership before migrations.
2. Add durable job, row error, lineage, and outbox storage through additive Flyway migrations. Expose BFF job creation and status, including counts, fatal errors, and paginated row errors. Set upload-size, row-count, timeout, and retention limits from the agreed operating envelope.
3. Implement the S3 event bridge, SQS dispatch and DLQ, and Temporal start. Exercise duplicate notifications, late events, ambiguous starts, and reconciliation before applying inventory.
4. Implement staging and atomic DELTA apply. Run the supplied CSV against PostgreSQL 18 and check replay, timestamp collisions, manual edits, forced overwrite, malformed quoting, duplicate IDs, lost staging, and worker failure immediately after commit.
5. Add scoped FULL_SNAPSHOT with a protected retirement calculation. Verify that malformed rows with IDs stay present, out-of-scope frames stay untouched, and the exact 5% and 10% boundaries behave as agreed. Exercise rejection of environment scopes without a region, expired and out-of-order watermarks, watermark equality, derived watermarks, newer ancestors rejecting narrower snapshots, newer descendants protecting entire subtrees while present rows still upsert, frames created or moved into scope after export, and concurrent manual writes. Roll out DELTA first, then enable snapshot after observing apply times and reviewing operator safeguards.
6. Track queue age and DLQ depth, time in each job state, staging retries, apply transaction duration, row error codes, retirement guard trips, and outbox lag. Correlate logs by job ID and keep presigned URLs and raw row content out of logs.

Introduction
Section titled “Introduction”
When you’re developing cloud and serverless applications, you need to grant access to various AWS resources like S3 buckets and RDS databases.
To handle this, you create IAM roles and assign permissions through policies.
However, configuring these policies can be challenging, especially if you want to ensure minimal access of all principals to your resources.
LocalStack IAM Policy Stream automates the generation of IAM policies for your AWS API requests on your local machine.
This stream helps you identify the necessary permissions for your cloud application and allows you to detect logical errors, such as unexpected actions in your policies.
This tutorial will guide you through setting up IAM Policy Stream for a locally running AWS application.
We’ll use a basic example involving an S3 bucket, an SQS queue, and a bucket notification configuration.
You’ll generate the policy for the bucket notification configuration and insert it into the SQS queue.
Why use IAM Policy Stream?
Section titled “Why use IAM Policy Stream?”
LocalStack enables you to create and enforce local IAM roles and policies using the
ENFORCE_IAM feature.
However, users often struggle to figure out the necessary permissions for different actions.
It’s important to find a balance, avoiding giving too many permissions while making sure the right ones are granted.
This challenge becomes more complex when dealing with AWS services that make requests not directly visible to users.
For instance, if an SNS topic sends a message to an SQS queue and the underlying call fails, there might be no clear error message, causing confusion, especially for those less familiar with the services.
IAM Policy Stream simplifies this by automatically generating the needed policies and showing them to users.
This makes it easier to integrate with resources, roles, and users, streamlining the development process.
Additionally, it serves as a useful learning tool, helping users understand the permissions linked to various AWS calls and improving the onboarding experience for newcomers to AWS.

LOCALSTACK_AUTH_TOKEN

Architecture diagram
Section titled “Architecture diagram”
The following diagram illustrates the architecture of this tutorial:
In this architecture:
An
S3 bucket is configured to send event notifications when objects are created
An
SQS queue receives these notifications
The
IAM Enforcement Engine intercepts API calls and checks for proper permissions
The
IAM Policy Stream Dashboard captures all API requests and generates the necessary IAM policies
When a file is uploaded to the S3 bucket, S3 attempts to send a message to SQS, which initially fails due to missing permissions
The IAM Policy Stream automatically generates the required policy, which can then be applied to resolve the violation
Tutorial: Configure an S3 bucket for event notifications using SQS
Section titled “Tutorial: Configure an S3 bucket for event notifications using SQS”
In this tutorial, you will configure a LocalStack S3 bucket to send event notifications to an SQS queue.
You will then use IAM Policy Stream to generate the necessary IAM policy for the SQS queue.
You will use Terraform to create the resources and the AWS CLI to interact with them.
With LocalStack’s IAM enforcement enabled, you can thoroughly test your policy and ensure that the development setup mirrors the production environment.

Generate a comprehensive policy
Section titled “Generate a comprehensive policy”
In scenarios where there are many AWS services, and every AWS API request generates a policy it might be cumbersome to analyze every policy.
In such cases, you can generate one comprehensive policy for all your AWS resources together.
You can navigate to the
Summary Policy tab on the IAM Policy Stream dashboard.
This concatenates the policy per principle which the policy should be attached to.
For the example above, you would be able to see the
Identity Policy for the root user which has all the actions and resources inside one single policy file for the operations we performed.
On the other hand, you have the
Resource Policy for the SQS queue, where you can see the permission necessary for the subscription.
For larger AWS applications, you would be able to find multiple roles and multiple resource-based policies depending on your scenario.

Verification Checklist
Section titled “Verification Checklist”
To ensure your IAM policies are correctly configured:
No IAM violations appear in the IAM Policy Stream dashboard
Messages are successfully delivered to the SQS queue
No new violation entries are logged for the
SendMessage operation after the policy is applied
All API calls display green checkmarks in the Policy Stream dashboard
Conclusion
Section titled “Conclusion”
IAM Policy Stream streamlines your development process by minimizing the manual creation of policies and confirming the necessity of granted permissions.
However, it is advisable to manually confirm that your policy aligns with your intended actions.
Your code may unintentionally make requests, and LocalStack considers all requests made during policy generation as valid.
A practical scenario is automating tests, such as integration or end-to-end testing, against your application using LocalStack.
This setup allows LocalStack to automatically generate policies with the required permissions.
However, it’s important to note that these generated policies may not cover all possible requests, as only the requests made during testing are included.
You can then review and customize the policies to meet your needs, ensuring that overly permissive policies don’t find their way into production environments.

Open [Frame Inventory BFF](http://127.0.0.1:3001/d/frame-inventory-bff/frame-inventory-bff) for GraphQL request rate, error percentage, p50/p95/p99 latency, in-flight requests, and event loop utilization. The **Slowest queries and mutations (p95)** panel ranks top-level fields such as `frames` and `updateFrame` by resolver latency over the selected time range. Run the [frame list query](./src/bff/README.md) several times across at least two scrapes. Run `{ frames(page: -1) { page } }` to generate a GraphQL error. The dashboard counts GraphQL errors even when Apollo responds with HTTP 200. ### Backend and BFF logs Run `docker compose up -d --build bff grafana`. Alloy reads the backend and BFF containers’ stdout and stderr through the Docker socket and sends them to Loki. Loki stores logs in the `loki-data` volume with seven-day retention. For a failed GraphQL request, take the `X-Correlation-Id` response header and search both services with `{service_name=~"backend|bff"} | json | correlationId="your-id"`. For a production deployment, configure log storage, retention, and access controls for that environment. Open [Grafana Explore](http://127.0.0.1:3001/explore), select **Loki**, and switch to **Code** mode to run either LogQL query. - Backend — `{service_name="backend"}` - BFF — `{service_name="bff"}` ### OpenTelemetry Collector Run `docker compose up -d --build otel-collector` to start the Collector and its dependencies. docs/designs/bulk-csv-inventory-import-design.md:9:Inventory operators can upload `inventory_frame.csv` from the running application and see the result as the job progresses. A routine update changes only the frames named in the file. An authoritative snapshot can also retire missing frames within a declared area of the inventory. Every accepted change is visible in frame history.
docs/designs/bulk-csv-inventory-import-design.md:17:- Let an authorized operator upload the supplied 45-field CSV from the application and see job progress, final counts, and actionable row errors.
docs/designs/bulk-csv-inventory-import-design.md:57:Re-read the current version under the existing stable-frame lock. A newer source timestamp creates a version. Equal timestamp and hash is a no-op. Skip and report stale rows and same-timestamp collisions unless forceOverwrite is authorized and set, and record both hashes for collisions. Manual writes set source_modified_at from database statement time after locking, and CSV writes preserve the input timestamp. For existing manual versions that inherited their source timestamp, use the version’s valid_from as the effective conflict baseline. Identify those versions at migration time and preserve the original source_modified_at for history. Forced corrections record FORCED_OVERWRITE and import_job_id. Subsequent imports compare against the current version’s source timestamp, including when a forced overwrite moves that timestamp backward. For example, an 11:00 row is newer after a forced overwrite replaces a 12:00 version with a 10:00 version. Use the same database-generated boundary for closing and opening a version, strictly later than the previous valid_from.
docs/designs/bulk-csv-inventory-import-design.md:59:When a frame has no current version and its latest version was closed by MANUAL_DELETE, require an authorized forceOverwrite to restore it in either import mode. Without that flag, skip the row and record MANUALLY_DELETED in the job’s row errors. With it, append a new current version, preserve the CSV source timestamp, and record FORCED_OVERWRITE and import_job_id in the apply transaction. Compare and restore under the stable-frame lock.
docs/designs/bulk-csv-inventory-import-design.md:81:**Rejected by author** — Send S3 notifications directly to the standard SQS queue to remove the forwarding hop.
docs/designs/bulk-csv-inventory-import-design.md:91:**Rejected by author** — Extend the existing versioned schema for this release. It already gives current and historical frames one authoritative store and preserves links and external references per version. A separate history store would add a second representation of those changes.

Create `inventoryimport/ImportJobService.java` to authorize the requested mode and force flag, validate canonical scope, create the job, and sign the exact S3 PUT. Create `inventoryimport/ImportJobRepository.java` for conditional job transitions, object binding, diagnostics, and returned outcomes.

Update [globals.css](../../src/frontend/src/app/globals.css) for the upload and results UI.
docs/designs/bulk-csv-inventory-import.md:10:The worker streams the CSV into job-scoped UNLOGGED PostgreSQL staging in batches and heartbeats during loading. It records invalid rows in import_row_errors and applies set-based writes with MERGE RETURNING where appropriate. The proposed six-table target and frame history must be reconciled with the repository's existing versioned schema. Inventory changes and outbox records must commit together.
docs/designs/bulk-csv-inventory-import.md:32:- Define the content hash over canonical typed values, including versioned links and external references. Specify normalization, timezone and precision, null behavior, and duplicate-ID handling. Change manual UI/API writes to set source_modified_at from statement_timestamp() on the version insert after obtaining the frame lock. Preserve the source timestamp on CSV imports, including forced overwrites. Define how comparisons handle legacy manual versions that inherited an older source timestamp. A forced overwrite can move the current source timestamp backward. A separate source high-water mark remains an open decision.
docs/designs/bulk-csv-inventory-import.md:33:- Build one candidate per target key before set-based writes. Resolve shared dimensions and reserve frame identities before opening dependent versions and links. PostgreSQL 18 supports MERGE RETURNING, but a source candidate takes only one action, so close and append in separate set-based statements in the same transaction. Use the actual changed version IDs to produce outbox records. Commit versions, links, outbox, and final job status together. A retry after a lost commit response returns the committed result. [PostgreSQL MERGE](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-merge.html)
docs/designs/bulk-csv-inventory-import.md:39:- Use canonical scope keys in a containment hierarchy: GLOBAL, country, country/region, and country/region/environment. Require a region for every environment-level FULL_SNAPSHOT in the first release. Reject a country/environment scope such as UK/UNDERGROUND at job creation. An operator can export a separate authoritative snapshot for each region or use DELTA for a cross-region file.
docs/designs/bulk-csv-inventory-import.md:50:- Deliver authenticated upload, visible job progress and row errors, retry-safe imports, audited versions, scoped retirement, and transactional outbox records.
docs/designs/bulk-csv-inventory-import.md:51:- Leave mass deletion, generalized CSV mapping, automatic repair of malformed source values, and multi-scope FULL_SNAPSHOT uploads outside the first release. If authoritative cross-region exports become a regular need, consider one atomic job over explicitly named scopes, each with its own watermark and retirement check.
docs/designs/bulk-csv-inventory-import.md:57:- Reuse versioned history as the initial design direction. Add a separate frame_history table only if it serves a distinct audited need. Otherwise two history stores would require agreement on which is authoritative.
docs/designs/bulk-csv-inventory-import.md:61:1. Map the CSV to the current schema and the proposed six entities. Resolve source timestamp parsing, manual-edit ordering, force authorization, link semantics, duplicate IDs, and schema ownership before migrations.
docs/designs/bulk-csv-inventory-import.md:62:2. Add durable job, row error, lineage, and outbox storage through additive Flyway migrations. Expose BFF job creation and status, including counts, fatal errors, and paginated row errors. Set upload-size, row-count, timeout, and retention limits from the agreed operating envelope.
docs/designs/bulk-csv-inventory-import.md:66:6. Track queue age and DLQ depth, time in each job state, staging retries, apply transaction duration, row error codes, retirement guard trips, and outbox lag. Correlate logs by job ID and keep presigned URLs and raw row content out of logs.

docs/designs/bulk-csv-inventory-import-design.md:9:Inventory operators can upload `inventory_frame.csv` from the running application and see the result as the job progresses. A routine update changes only the frames named in the file. An authoritative snapshot can also retire missing frames within a declared area of the inventory. Every accepted change is visible in frame history.
docs/designs/bulk-csv-inventory-import-design.md:17:- Let an authorized operator upload the supplied 45-field CSV from the application and see job progress, final counts, and actionable row errors.
docs/designs/bulk-csv-inventory-import-design.md:57:Re-read the current version under the existing stable-frame lock. A newer source timestamp creates a version. Equal timestamp and hash is a no-op. Skip and report stale rows and same-timestamp collisions unless forceOverwrite is authorized and set, and record both hashes for collisions. Manual writes set source_modified_at from database statement time after locking, and CSV writes preserve the input timestamp. For existing manual versions that inherited their source timestamp, use the version’s valid_from as the effective conflict baseline. Identify those versions at migration time and preserve the original source_modified_at for history. Forced corrections record FORCED_OVERWRITE and import_job_id. Subsequent imports compare against the current version’s source timestamp, including when a forced overwrite moves that timestamp backward. For example, an 11:00 row is newer after a forced overwrite replaces a 12:00 version with a 10:00 version. Use the same database-generated boundary for closing and opening a version, strictly later than the previous valid_from.
docs/designs/bulk-csv-inventory-import-design.md:59:When a frame has no current version and its latest version was closed by MANUAL_DELETE, require an authorized forceOverwrite to restore it in either import mode. Without that flag, skip the row and record MANUALLY_DELETED in the job’s row errors. With it, append a new current version, preserve the CSV source timestamp, and record FORCED_OVERWRITE and import_job_id in the apply transaction. Compare and restore under the stable-frame lock.

It decodes the key and verifies the bucket, key, object version, and size, then conditionally records PENDING and starts Temporal workflow csv-import-{jobId}. Duplicate or out-of-order records must preserve the existing object binding and job state. Acknowledge the message after each applicable record has been handled, including confirming successful or already-completed workflow dispatch. If processing a later record fails, replay of earlier records uses the same job and workflow identities. Retry with backoff. Before a DLQ event can fail a job, reconcile ambiguous workflow starts and check that the job is still dispatchable. Reconcile old AWAITING_UPLOAD and PENDING jobs against S3 and Temporal.
47:Accept files up to 10 MiB and 10,000 data rows, whichever limit is reached first. Verify object size before dispatch and enforce both limits while streaming. The header does not count. Exceeding either limit fails the job before inventory writes. Keep uploaded object versions and row diagnostics for 7 days. Keep the minimal durable job outcome and import lineage available to history after diagnostics expire. Bound retries and reconciliation within the object retention period.

Preserve direct and history lookups.

Create [inventory-import.tsx](../../src/frontend/src/app/inventory-import.tsx) to collect mode and scope, submit the presigned PUT with its required headers, poll the job, and show progress and errors. content.text:
The design addresses the exercise’s core requirement with an operator-driven import, visible results, and a single authoritative version history. Resolve two blockers before treating the full design as ready.

| Priority | Scope | Finding and proposed resolution |
|---|---|---|
| Blocker | Snapshot apply, lines 67–69 | The design requires rejection of incomplete exports without defining evidence of completeness. A file truncated after a valid record can reach EOF, produce a watermark, and omit fewer frames than the 10% retirement limit. Require trusted producer metadata that binds the declared scope, export time, expected record count, and uploaded bytes. Keep snapshot retirement disabled until the producer can supply that evidence. |
| Blocker | Upload, lines 17, 41, 108, 118 | The plan assumes operator authorization already flows through the BFF. The current request context contains only a correlation ID, and the backend interceptor handles tracing. Specify the trusted identity source, how Spring verifies it, and who may create imports, submit snapshots, force changes, or read another operator’s job and row diagnostics. |
| Major | Snapshot reactivation, lines 67–73 | Only unchanged reactivation is explicitly gated. If retirement preserves the last live source timestamp, a parent snapshot at 11:30 can present a 09:00 row and reverse a child snapshot’s 12:00 retirement of the 08:00 version under the ordinary newer-row rule. Persist the retirement’s export watermark and define how every reactivation path, including DELTA and force, relates to it. Comparing the next export to the retirement’s commit time can also reject a legitimately later export taken before that commit. |
| Major | Goals and inventory transaction, lines 18, 61 | The source RFC calls for transactional outbox records, and the draft promises duplicate-free events. The draft’s transaction, migration, and tests omit events. Identify their consumer and include the outbox in the atomic apply, or explicitly record the decision to remove the event requirement. |
| Major | Dispatch and staging, lines 30–51, 83–85 | Direct S3-to-SQS removes the forwarding Lambda. SQS plus Temporal still creates two retry systems and a reconciliation boundary for a 1,000-row fixture with a 10 MiB maximum. Record the requirement served by each service. If both are fixed scope, logged staging is a simpler starting point because it avoids crash-induced restaging and completion recovery. Choose unlogged staging if measurements justify it. |
| Major | Inventory writes, lines 55–61, 108–112 | The dedicated bulk repository may duplicate existing stable-frame locking, validity-boundary calculation, dimension resolution, and versioned-child handling in `FrameRepository`.
